Dashcam, head unit, lights: wiring them in properly
How to connect a dashcam, a USB charger, a head unit and auxiliary lights without burning the wiring or causing faults in the car.

You can connect a dashcam, a USB charger, a head unit or auxiliary lights yourself. The main rule: every new load gets its own fuse, and the wire must handle more than that fuse. When running wires from the battery, disconnect the clamp from the negative terminal first.
Work out the current and choose the wire

Current is power divided by voltage. A 5 W dashcam draws less than half an amp. A pair of 55 W lights draws about 110 / 12 ≈ 9 A. The fuse is chosen about a quarter higher than the working current and rounded up to a standard rating: for these lights, 15 A. And the wire gauge is chosen to match the fuse, not the load.

These are conservative figures for stranded copper wire up to 3 m long: 5 A — 0,75 mm², 10 A — 1,5 mm², 15 A — 2,5 mm², 25 A — 4 mm². For a longer wire, or one in a shared harness, go one size thicker. Cheap copper-clad aluminum wire (CCA) of the same thickness carries less current.
Fuse on the positive side, at the source

The fuse goes in the positive wire as close as possible to where you take the power from — the battery or the fuse box. If the wire chafes through against the body, the fuse blows and saves the wiring. If the fuse sits next to the load, the whole wire up to it is unprotected.

Powerful loads — lights, a compressor — are switched through a relay: a switch in the cabin controls the coil (85 and 86), and the high current flows through contacts 30 and 87 over a short, thick wire. How a relay works is covered in the lesson on fuses and relays.
Tapping in with a fuse tap
A dashcam and a USB charger are easy to power from the fuse box with a fuse tap. It plugs into the slot in place of the factory fuse and holds two fuses: the factory one and a new one for your wire.
Buy a fuse tap for your type of fuses: standard, mini or low-profile.
Choose a non-critical circuit that’s powered through the ignition switch, such as the cigarette lighter. That way the dashcam won’t drain the battery while the car is parked.
Pull out the factory fuse, switch on the ignition and use a multimeter to find which side of the slot has 12 V — that’s the power side.
Insert the fuse tap with the blade shared by both fuses on the power side. Put the factory fuse of the same rating into it, plus a new one sized for the device’s current.
Ground goes to the nearest body bolt.

Don’t take power from the airbag (SRS), ABS, engine control unit or fuel pump circuits — neither with a fuse tap nor by splicing into a wire. A fuse tap is only for small things like a dashcam or a charger.
Ground and head unit

The negative goes to bare body metal under a factory bolt, or to the battery negative, with a ring terminal. Plastic, paint and a random self-tapping screw are not a ground: the contact will heat up and the device will glitch.

In a standard ISO connector, the yellow wire is constant positive for memory, the red is switched positive from the ignition, and the black is ground. If both positives are connected to constant power, the head unit will drain the battery. Many cars, especially Japanese ones, have their own connector — buy an adapter for your model instead of cutting the factory wiring.
What not to do
Twisted joints under electrical tape: they corrode, heat up and burn through. Join wires with crimped butt connectors or with solder and heat-shrink tubing.
Connecting to airbag wires, usually in yellow sheathing or with yellow connectors.
Tapping into the CAN bus — a pair of wires twisted together: you’ll get fault codes, and the car may not start.
Taking power or a “control positive” from sensor and control unit signal wires.
Running a wire over sharp edges and through doors without protection; laying the dashcam wire over the curtain airbag in the pillar — route it along the factory harness.
Every new load gets its own fuse in the positive wire, as close to the source as possible.
Current = power / voltage; the wire gauge is chosen to match the fuse.
Powerful loads go through a relay; small ones through a fuse tap in a non-critical circuit switched by the ignition.
Ground goes to clean body metal or the battery negative, with a ring terminal.
No twisted joints, and no tapping into airbags, the CAN bus or sensor wires.
Where does the fuse for a new load go?
In the negative wire, next to the load
In the positive wire, as close to the power source as possible
Nowhere, if the wire is thick
A fuse protects the wire. Placed at the source, it protects the wire along its whole length: if the wire chafes through against the body, the fuse blows before the wiring catches fire.
A pair of 55 W auxiliary lights. Roughly how much current do they draw from a 12 V system?
About 1 A
About 55 A
About 9 A
About 110 A
Current is power divided by voltage: 110 W / 12 V ≈ 9 A. The fuse for them is 15 A, the wire 2,5 mm².
A dashcam was connected with a fuse tap to a circuit that has power all the time. What’s the risk?
The dashcam may drain the battery while the car is parked
None — it’s even better that way
The dashcam will burn out right away
A constant-power circuit stays live even with the engine off. For a dashcam, choose a circuit powered through the ignition switch.
What’s the right way to join wires when connecting something?
Twist them together under electrical tape
Splice into a CAN bus wire
To the airbag connector
With a crimped butt connector, or solder and heat-shrink tubing
A twisted joint corrodes and heats up over time. Crimping, or soldering with heat-shrink tubing, gives a reliable, protected contact.
Lighting: bulbs, LED, xenon and headlight aim
Which bulbs your headlights use and how to replace them, why you can’t put xenon or LED bulbs in halogen headlights, where the “bulb out” error comes from, and how to check headlight aim.
Drivers can replace most bulbs themselves. But with lighting “upgrades” it’s easy to blind oncoming drivers and break the law.
Bases and bulbs
The bulb type is given in the owner’s manual, on the bulb itself and often on the headlight housing. The most common ones:
H4 — two filaments in one bulb, low and high beam, 60/55 W.
H7, H1, H11 — one filament each, 55 W: low beam, high beam or fog lights.
W5W — a small wedge-base bulb: parking lights, license plate light.
P21W — turn signals, brake lights, reverse lights; P21/5W — dual-filament, brake light and parking light in one bulb; PY21W — amber, for turn signals.
D1S, D2S, D2R, D4S and others with the letter D — factory xenon.
How to replace them
Switch off the lights and the ignition, and let the bulb cool down.
Unplug the connector, remove the protective cap and release the retaining clip.
Hold the new bulb by the base, not the glass: fingerprints make the glass overheat, and the bulb soon burns out.
Seat the bulb exactly in its slots, or the beam will point off to the side, and check that it works.

Replace bulbs in pairs: old ones are dimmer and a different shade. “+50 %” and “+100 %” bulbs of the same 55 W are acceptable if they carry a certification mark — the letter E in a circle — but they don’t last as long. Higher-wattage bulbs, such as 100 W instead of 55, must not be fitted: they melt the headlight and overheat the wiring.
Check the fuses first. If both headlights or both parking lights are out at once, the problem is most likely not the bulbs but a fuse or a relay.
Only touch a xenon bulb and its ballast with the lights off and the connector unplugged: at switch-on there are tens of thousands of volts there, as in the safety lesson.
Xenon and LED in factory headlights

A headlight is designed for its own light source. The lens or housing is marked: the letter H (for example, HC, HCR) means halogen, the letter D (DC, DCR) means xenon. The glowing part of a xenon or LED bulb sits in a different place from a halogen filament, and the reflector spreads the light incorrectly: the road is lit worse, and oncoming drivers are blinded.

In Kazakhstan, xenon or LED bulbs in headlights not designed for them count as unauthorized modification: a fine of 15 MCI (monthly calculation index) under Part 7 of Article 590 of the Code of Administrative Offenses of the Republic of Kazakhstan, and the car can be sent to an impound lot until the factory lighting is restored. The legal route is headlights originally designed for xenon or LED, properly registered according to the rules.

On right-hand-drive cars, the headlights are designed for left-hand traffic: the low-beam cutoff rises to the left, straight into the eyes of oncoming drivers. Such headlights are replaced with ones for right-hand traffic; some can be readjusted — check with a mechanic.
Why LEDs trigger a “bulb out” error

The body control unit monitors the current of each bulb. A 21 W halogen bulb draws about 1,75 A; an LED replacement draws many times less. The unit decides the bulb has burned out: a warning appears on the dashboard, the turn signals flash faster, and the LED may flicker from the unit’s test pulses.

So-called “error cancellers” are sold — load resistors and bulbs marked CANbus. A resistor turns the excess current into heat and gets very hot: never mount it on plastic or wires. Factory bulbs or a mechanic are a safer bet — sometimes the unit can be reconfigured with a scan tool.
Headlight aim

Use the headlight leveling knob on the dashboard to lower the beams when the car is loaded; which position suits which load is in the owner’s manual. You can roughly check the aim against a wall: level ground, normal tire pressure, the leveler at “0”, the car 5 m from the wall. Mark the height of the headlight centers on the wall: the low-beam cutoff should be below it. If the headlight is marked with a 1 % tilt, at 5 m that’s 5 cm. Headlights are aimed precisely at a service station with an aiming device.
The bulb type is in the owner’s manual and on the bulb; hold halogen bulbs by the base and replace them in pairs.
Both headlights out at once — check the fuse and relay first.
Xenon and LED only in headlights designed for them; otherwise they blind oncoming drivers and can get you a 15 MCI fine.
LEDs in a factory circuit trigger an error because of their low current; “error canceller” resistors get very hot.
The low-beam cutoff is below the headlight centers: with a 1 % tilt, 5 cm lower at 5 m.
Why shouldn’t you touch the glass of a halogen bulb with your fingers?
Fingerprints make the glass overheat, and the bulb soon burns out
You could get an electric shock
The bulb will start glowing blue
The greasy mark creates a hot spot on the glass. The glass overheats, and the bulb burns out much sooner than it should.
Can you put LED bulbs in a headlight marked HCR?
Yes, if the base fits
No: the headlight is designed for halogen, LEDs blind oncoming drivers, and you can be fined for it
Yes, if you add a resistor
The letter H means the headlight is designed for halogen bulbs. With a different light source it spreads the light incorrectly, and in Kazakhstan this counts as unauthorized modification.
After LEDs were fitted in the turn signals, they flash faster and there’s a warning on the dashboard. Why?
The alternator has burned out
The wrong LED color
Positive and negative are mixed up
The LED draws little current, and the control unit thinks the bulb has burned out
The control unit or the turn signal relay monitors the current. An LED draws many times less than a halogen bulb, and the electronics take this as a burned-out bulb.
Both low-beam headlights are out at once. What should you check first?
Buy new headlights
The headlight leveler position
The low-beam fuse and relay
Two bulbs rarely burn out at the same time. The common cause for both is a fuse, a relay or the power supply.
Electrical checklist: before a trip and before winter
What to check in your car’s electrical system before a long trip and before winter, and what kit to carry with you.

Most roadside breakdowns start with something small you could have spotted at home: a corroded terminal, a cracked belt, a burned-out bulb. Twenty minutes of checks before a trip or before winter will save you a long wait on the side of the road.
Battery and terminals
Voltage after sitting overnight: 12,6–12,9 V. At about 12,4 V or below, charge it before the trip.
With the engine running: 13,5–14,5 V, including with the headlights and the heater on. If it’s lower, check the alternator before you set off.
The terminals shouldn’t turn by hand. If there’s a white or green coating, remove the clamp, clean it with a brush, wipe it with a baking soda solution and tighten it.
The battery is firmly secured and doesn’t move around.
A battery usually lasts 3–5 years. If yours is more than 4 years old or has already let you down, have a mechanic check it with a load tester before winter.
Alternator belt

Cracks across the ribs, peeling layers, a shiny “glazed” surface — it’s time to replace the belt. A squeal when starting in the cold or when a load is switched on means the belt is slipping: low tension, a worn tensioner or a worn belt. A snapped belt means a draining battery, and on many cars the water pump stops too and the engine overheats. If the battery light comes on while you’re driving, the alternator isn’t charging, as in the lesson on dashboard warning lights.
Inspect the belt only with the engine off and the ignition off: the radiator fan can switch on by itself. Keep your hands away from the belt and pulleys of a running engine.
Lights and fuses

Walk around the car: low and high beams, parking lights, turn signals, hazard lights, brake lights, reverse lights, license plate light, fog lights. Someone can help you check the brake lights, or you can look at their reflection in a shop window in the evening. Take spare bulbs of your types, as in the lighting lesson.

Put spare fuses of your type — standard, mini or low-profile — and a pair of tweezers in the glove box. Take photos of the diagrams on the fuse box lids with your phone: in the dark and the cold, it’s quicker that way.
Check the fuses first. Many roadside “breakdowns” are fixed in five minutes with a spare fuse of the same rating.
Before winter — extra checks
Fully charge the battery with a charger, even if the car starts.
On a diesel — glow plugs, winter fuel and the filter, as in the lesson on winter starting.
Run the parking heater before the cold sets in, so any faults show up now and not at −30 °C.
Check the heater fan at all speeds, the window and mirror heating, the wipers and the washer, and fill up with winter washer fluid.
Replace the key fob battery if its range has got worse.
What to take with you

Jumper cables 3–4 m long with copper conductors: from 16 mm² for a car, from 25 mm² for a diesel or an SUV. Cheap cables have thick insulation but a thin conductor — look at the copper, not the sheathing.
A jump starter (booster) — charged. In winter, keep it inside the car: lithium jump starters get noticeably weaker in the cold.
A multimeter or a test light, spare fuses and bulbs.
A headlamp, gloves, electrical tape, cable ties and a wrench for the battery terminals — on many cars it’s a 10 mm.
A phone charger for the cigarette lighter socket, a tow rope, warm clothes. A fire extinguisher, a first-aid kit and a warning triangle are mandatory.
Battery: 12,6–12,9 V at rest and 13,5–14,5 V while driving; the terminals are clean and don’t turn.
A belt with no cracks, glazing or squeal; inspect it only with the engine off.
All the lights work; spare bulbs and fuses are in the car.
Before winter — fully charge the battery and check the parking heater, glow plugs and heating functions.
For the road — thick copper jumper cables or a jump starter, a flashlight, a multimeter, tools.
Before winter, the battery reads 12,3 V after sitting overnight. What should you do?
Nothing, that’s normal
Charge it with a charger and check again
Replace the alternator right away
Full charge is 12,6–12,9 V. At 12,3 V the battery is noticeably discharged, and in freezing weather it will need all the reserve it has.
The alternator belt squeals when starting in the cold. What does that mean?
That’s normal in winter
The battery is dead
The belt is slipping: tension, the tensioner or a worn belt
A squeal means slipping. If the cause isn’t fixed, the alternator will undercharge the battery, and the belt may snap.
Which jumper cables should you take for a diesel SUV?
Copper, with a cross-section of 25 mm² or more
Any thin ones, as long as they’re long
With thick sheathing; the cross-section doesn’t matter
A diesel needs a lot of current to start. A thin conductor under thick insulation heats up and can’t carry it.
How do you inspect the alternator belt safely?
At idle, so you can see it slipping
With the ignition on
Holding the belt with your hand while the engine runs
With the engine off and the ignition off
On a running engine, the belt can pull your hand in, and with the ignition on, the radiator fan can switch on by itself.
Starter motor: design and testing
How the starter and its control circuit work, and how to use voltage drop and cranking current to tell a faulty starter from bad wiring.

The starter is the most powerful load in the car: it draws hundreds of amps while cranking. That’s why a few extra hundredths of an ohm in its circuit immediately turn into slow cranking. The diagnostician’s job is to work out whether the starter itself, its power supply or its control circuit is to blame.
How it’s built
Electric motor: an armature with a commutator, brushes, and a stator with field windings or permanent magnets.

The solenoid on the housing. It has two windings — pull-in and hold-in. Through a shift fork, the solenoid pushes the pinion into mesh with the flywheel ring gear and, at the end of its travel, closes the main contacts (the “contact discs”) between terminal 30 and the motor.
The Bendix drive is a pinion with an overrunning clutch. Once the engine starts, the clutch slips and keeps the engine from overspinning the armature.
Gear-reduction starter: a planetary gearset sits between the motor and the pinion; the motor is small and fast, often with permanent magnets. This type of starter is lighter and draws less current.
Control circuit

A heavy power cable runs from the battery to terminal 30, usually with no fuse. Terminal 50 gets positive from the ignition switch, and on most modern cars it comes through a starter relay controlled by the ignition switch, the body control module or the ECU. Interlocks are wired into the circuit: the automatic transmission range switch (starting only in P or N), on many cars a clutch pedal switch, and on cars with a start button, the brake pedal.
The battery is charged: 12,4–12,9 V at rest. With a discharged battery, there’s no point measuring any further.

To keep the engine from starting during the measurements, disable the fuel supply as the manual describes — for example, pull the fuel pump fuse or relay. Set the parking brake and put the automatic in P.
Terminal 50: with the key in START, the voltage is almost the same as at the battery while cranking. No positive — look in the control circuit: fuse, relay, interlocks, ignition switch.

Drop on the positive side while cranking (as in the multimeter lesson): from the battery’s positive post to terminal 30 — up to 0,5 V. On the ground side: from the starter housing to the battery’s negative post — up to 0,2–0,3 V.
Battery voltage while cranking — no lower than about 9,6–10 V.

Cranking current — measure it with a clamp meter on the power cable. For gasoline passenger cars it’s usually around 100–200 A, more for diesels; the spec is in the manual. Shacman, Howo and KAMAZ trucks have a 24 V system with their own specs.

High current and slow cranking — mechanical resistance: bushings, a short in the armature, a tight engine. Low current and slow cranking — resistance in the circuit: terminals, wires, the “contact discs”, brushes.
A click with no rotation: burnt solenoid contacts, worn or stuck brushes, a “dead spot” on the commutator.
The starter whirs but doesn’t turn the engine: the overrunning clutch is slipping or the pinion isn’t coming out. The fix is to replace the Bendix drive and inspect the ring gear teeth.
Grinding or seizing in a gear-reduction starter — the gearset has failed or a magnet has come unglued.
The starter keeps cranking after the key is released — the solenoid contacts are stuck closed. Turn off the ignition; if it keeps spinning, disconnect the battery negative.
If it cranks after a few taps, the starter is worn and due for repair: brushes, solenoid contacts, bushings.

Disconnect the battery negative before removing the starter: terminal 30 is always live, and a wrench touching the housing will cause a short of hundreds of amps — burns and fire. Don’t run the starter by bridging terminals 30 and 50 with a screwdriver: this bypasses the interlocks, and a car in gear will drive off. Crank for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with 30–60 second pauses.
The solenoid pushes the Bendix drive into mesh and closes the main contacts from 30 to the motor.
No positive at 50 when starting — look in the control circuit: relay, automatic transmission and clutch interlocks, ignition switch.
While cranking: up to 0,5 V on the positive side, up to 0,2–0,3 V on the ground side, battery no lower than about 9,6–10 V.
High current and slow — mechanical; low current and slow — resistance in the circuit.
With the key turned to START, there’s no voltage at starter terminal 50. Where should you look?
In the starter brushes
In the Bendix overrunning clutch
In the control circuit: fuse, starter relay, transmission or clutch interlock, ignition switch
Terminal 50 is the control input. If positive doesn’t reach it, the starter itself isn’t to blame: the cause is in the circuit leading to it.
The starter cranks slowly, the cranking current is noticeably above spec, and the drops on the positive and ground sides are normal. What is most likely?
Mechanical resistance: bushings, a short in the armature or an engine that’s hard to turn
A corroded battery terminal
An open in the terminal 50 wire
A bad contact would reduce the current. High current with slow rotation means the motor is struggling to turn.
The starter whirs loudly, but the engine doesn’t turn over. What is most likely faulty?
Starter relay
The Bendix overrunning clutch or the pinion engagement mechanism
Control circuit fuse
Battery
The starter motor spins, so power and control are fine. The rotation isn’t reaching the flywheel.
How do you measure the voltage drop on the starter ground?
Red lead on terminal 30, black on terminal 50
Both leads on the starter housing with the ignition off
Red on the battery negative, black on the body, with no load
Red on the starter housing, black on the battery’s negative post — while cranking
The drop is measured under load, between the load’s housing and the battery negative. With no current flowing, a bad contact doesn’t show up.
Ignition and misfires
How modern ignition works, how to find the misfiring cylinder and tell what’s to blame: the coil, the spark plug, the wiring or the mechanical side.

Misfires are one of the most common complaints: the engine runs rough, jerks under load, and the “Check Engine” light comes on or flashes. The cause can be ignition, fuel or mechanical. The goal isn’t to replace everything in sight, but to find the cause in a few checks.
What’s on the engine
Individual coils — one for each spark plug. The most common setup on modern Toyota, Hyundai, Kia and Chinese cars.
A module or twin coils serving two cylinders, with high-voltage leads — “wasted spark”: the spark fires in two cylinders at once, and one of them is on its exhaust stroke.

A coil with two terminals has no igniter: the ECU itself switches the ground of the primary winding. One with three or four terminals usually has a built-in igniter: positive, ground, the control signal from the ECU, and sometimes a spark confirmation signal (IGF on Toyota). Pin functions — only from the wiring diagram.
Spark plugs

Type, gap and heat range — strictly per the manual or catalog. Heat range scales differ between manufacturers, some even run in opposite directions, so you can’t compare plugs from different brands “by the number”.
Check the gap with a round wire gauge. Plugs with a fine iridium or platinum electrode are usually installed with the factory gap; don’t bend the center electrode. Tightening torque — per the manual.

Read the insulator: light brown — normal; dry black soot — rich mixture or weak spark; wet with fuel — the cylinder is misfiring; oil — worn rings or valve stem seals; white and blistered — overheating; a crack or a flashover “track” — replace the plug.
How to find misfires

Read the codes: P0300 — misfires in random or multiple cylinders, P0301–P0306 — a misfire in the cylinder whose number is the last digit. A flashing “Check Engine” light means misfires bad enough to overheat the catalytic converter: don’t keep driving like that for long.
Look at the freeze frame — the rpm, load and temperature at which the misfires appeared — and the per-cylinder misfire counters, if your scan tool shows them.
Inspect the spark plug wells: oil from under the valve cover gasket or water after a car wash destroys the coil boots.
Swap the coils of the suspect cylinder and a neighboring one, as in the lesson on actuators. If the misfire follows the coil, the coil is to blame. If it stays, swap the spark plugs the same way.
If the misfire stays put, check the injector and its wiring, the compression and the valves.
Checking the coil circuits
Positive at the coil connector — with the ignition on or while cranking. Check the ground by voltage drop under load, relative to the battery negative.
The signal from the ECU to a coil with an igniter — check it with an LED test light or an oscilloscope while cranking: you should see even pulses.

In the primary circuit of a coil without an igniter, spikes of hundreds of volts occur when the circuit opens. Don’t connect an LED test light or a test lamp there — only an oscilloscope with an attenuator.
No signal at all the coils at once — check the crankshaft position sensor and the ECU’s power supply and grounds.

The secondary circuit carries tens of thousands of volts. Remove coils only with the ignition off, don’t hold the leads by hand with the engine running, and don’t check for spark “to ground” without a spark tester: the spark will find a path through the insulation and damage the coil and the ECU, and the shock is dangerous — especially for people with a pacemaker.
P0300 — misfires in multiple cylinders, P0301–P0306 — the cylinder number is the last digit.
Flashing “Check Engine” — severe misfires, the catalytic converter is at risk.
Swapping coils and spark plugs shows whether the fault follows the part.
Spark plug gap and heat range — only per the manual or catalog.
The secondary circuit carries tens of kilovolts: remove coils with the ignition off and check for spark with a spark tester.
What does code P0304 mean?
Misfires in cylinder 4
Misfires in multiple cylinders
The cylinder 4 coil is faulty
The code points to misfires in a cylinder, not to a part. The coil, spark plug, injector or compression could be to blame.
The coils of cylinders 2 and 3 were swapped, and code P0302 changed to P0303. What’s faulty?
The cylinder 2 spark plug
The cylinder 3 injector
The coil that used to be on cylinder 2
ECU
The misfire moved with the coil, so the coil is the problem.
Why can’t you choose the heat range by comparing the numbers on plugs from different manufacturers?
That number means the gap
Manufacturers use different scales, sometimes opposite ones — choose only by the catalog or manual
Heat range doesn’t affect anything
For one brand a higher number means a colder plug, for another a hotter one. A mistake leads to carbon fouling or overheating.
How do you safely check for spark?
Hold the lead near the body with your hand
Remove the coil with the engine running
Measure the resistance of a coil with a built-in igniter
Connect a spark tester to the coil and crank the engine
A spark tester gives the spark a safe path. An ohmmeter won’t tell you anything about a coil with an igniter.
Fuel injection, ECU power and grounds
Where the engine ECU gets its power, how to check the main relay, grounds, injectors and fuel pump, and how to work on the module without damaging it.
Many “faulty” ECUs are actually fine: they’re short of power or ground. Before looking for the cause in the sensors and injectors, make sure the module is properly powered.
How the engine module is powered
+30 — constant positive from the battery through a fuse. It keeps the memory alive: adaptations and trouble codes.
+15 — positive after the ignition switch. For the module, this is the “wake up” command.

The main relay. On many cars, once the ECU gets +15, it switches on the relay coil itself, and power from contact 87 goes to the module and to the injectors, coils, oxygen sensor heaters and sensors. After the ignition is turned off, the module keeps the relay on for a few seconds or longer — to save data and keep the fan running for a while.

The fuel pump relay is also switched by the ECU. On many cars, when the ignition is switched on, the pump runs for 2–3 seconds and shuts off if the module doesn’t see the crankshaft turning. Some cars have a fuel pump control module instead of a relay.
Engine and body grounds

An ECU usually has several grounds: power grounds for the injectors and coils, and signal grounds. Many sensors get their ground and 5 V reference from the module itself: don’t short these wires to the body. The engine, body and battery negative are connected by ground straps. A corroded or broken strap causes intermittent codes from many sensors at once.
Measure under load: while cranking, or with the engine running and the headlights and fan on.
Module ground: red lead on the ground pin of the ECU connector from the wire side, black on the battery’s negative post. Normal is hundredths of a volt; more than 0,1 V — look for a bad contact.
Engine ground: red lead on the cylinder block, black on the battery negative, while cranking. Guideline — up to 0,2–0,3 V.
+B supply with the relay on — almost the same as at the battery. A noticeable difference — look for losses section by section: fuse, the 30–87 contact, connector.
Positive comes from the main relay; the ECU switches the ground. Resistance — per the manual; injectors on the same engine should read almost the same.
The pulse from the ECU — check it with an injector noid light while cranking or with an oscilloscope, as in the oscilloscope lesson. Pulse width — per the manual and live data.
No pulses at any injector — check the main relay, the ECU’s power and grounds, the crankshaft sensor signal and immobilizer codes. None at one injector — check its wire and the module pin.
Fuel pump
The sequence: fuse and relay, then positive and ground at the pump connector under load, current with a clamp meter and fuel pressure with a gauge — specs per the manual.

The fuel in the lines is under pressure. Relieve the pressure as the manual describes, don’t disconnect the line while the pump is running, keep a fire extinguisher nearby and don’t allow sparks near fuel.
How not to damage the ECU
Disconnect and connect the module connector only with the ignition off and the battery negative disconnected.
Discharge static by touching body ground; on the bench, wear an antistatic wrist strap.
Don’t pierce the insulation with needles unless you have to: come in with a thin probe from the wire side through the seal, or use a breakout adapter. If you did pierce it, seal it.
Don’t connect a test lamp to ECU pins and sensor circuits, and don’t apply 12 V to 5 V circuits.
The ECU is powered from +30, +15 and the main relay; on many cars the module switches the relay itself.
ECU ground under load — hundredths of a volt; more than 0,1 V — a bad contact.
No pulses at any of the injectors — first check power, grounds and the crankshaft sensor.
ECU connector — only with the ignition off; don’t pierce wires with needles unless necessary, and don’t connect a test lamp to the pins.
What does the ECU need constant positive +30 for?
To crank the starter
To keep its memory: adaptations and trouble codes
To switch on the fan
+30 is always present, even with the ignition off. It keeps the module’s memory alive.
The voltage drop between the ECU ground pin and the battery negative while cranking is 0,6 V. What does that mean?
A bad contact in the ground circuit — track it down section by section
That’s normal for an ECU ground
The ECU is faulty and needs replacing
A weak battery
Normal is hundredths of a volt. 0,6 V points to a corroded ground strap, a loose nut or a bad contact in the connector.
While cranking, there are no pulses at any injector. Where do you start?
Replace all the injectors
Clean the injectors on a test bench
Check the main relay, the ECU’s power and grounds, and the crankshaft sensor signal
Injectors don’t all fail at once. The common cause is in the module’s power supply, or the module isn’t seeing the engine turn.
What is the right way to tap into a signal at the ECU connector?
Pierce the insulation with a needle and leave it like that
Connect a 21 W test lamp
Unplug the connector with the ignition on
With a thin probe from the wire side through the seal, or through a breakout adapter
That way you don’t damage the wire, the socket or the module output.
Scan tool and live data
How OBD-II diagnostics works, what the freeze frame, readiness monitors and fuel trims tell you, and how to use live data to prove the repair worked.
A scan tool doesn’t tell you what’s broken. It shows what the module sees: codes, the conditions they appeared under, and live sensor data. The conclusions are yours to draw.
Connector and protocols

The OBD-II connector has 16 pins and is usually under the dashboard near the steering wheel. 4 and 5 are grounds, 16 is battery positive, 6 and 14 are CAN, 7 is K-line, as in the lesson on data buses.
Protocols: CAN (ISO 15765) — on most cars since the late 2000s; on older ones — K-line (ISO 9141-2, ISO 14230) and SAE J1850 (pins 2 and 10). The scan tool usually detects the protocol by itself.
Generic OBD-II mode shows only what’s related to emissions: the engine and sometimes the transmission. ABS, airbags, body — only in the manufacturer-specific mode.
Right-hand-drive Japanese domestic-market cars may have the same connector, but generic OBD-II isn’t always supported — select the make and model in your scan tool.

Shacman, Howo and KAMAZ trucks with Weichai and Cummins engines have a 24 V system, usually the SAE J1939 protocol, and SPN/FMI codes (decoding is in the “Error codes” tab). The scan tool must be rated for 24 V.
Codes: record first, then clear

A confirmed code means the fault has been confirmed. A pending code means the module has noticed a deviation but hasn’t confirmed it yet. Many cars also have permanent codes: a scan tool can’t clear them, and the module removes them itself once the system passes its self-test.
Clearing deletes the codes and freeze frames and resets the readiness monitors. Clear them for no reason and you lose the evidence, and the fault will come back.
First save a report for all modules, clear the codes after the repair, and check whether the fault has come back.
Freeze frame and readiness monitors
The freeze frame is a snapshot of data at the moment the code was set: rpm, load, engine temperature, speed, fuel trims. You use it to recreate the conditions on a test drive.

Readiness monitors are the module’s self-tests: catalytic converter, oxygen sensors and their heaters, evaporative emissions, misfire, fuel system. Statuses: “ready”, “not ready”, “not supported”. After the codes are cleared or the battery is disconnected, the monitors need a drive cycle — per the manual. If a car you’re asked to “just take a look at” has all monitors “not ready”, the codes were most likely cleared recently.
Fuel trims

STFT is the short-term fuel trim: it swings quickly around zero based on the oxygen sensor signal. LTFT is the long-term trim: what the module has “learned”. Plus means the module is adding fuel because it sees a lean mixture; minus means it’s taking fuel away because it sees a rich one. Judge the sum STFT + LTFT on a warm engine in closed loop.
Within about ±10% is normal.
A large plus at idle that gets smaller at higher rpm — air leaking in past the MAF sensor.
A large plus under load — not enough fuel (pump, filter, pressure) or the MAF sensor is under-reading airflow.
A large minus — too much fuel: a leaking injector, high pressure — or the MAF sensor is over-reading.

On a V engine, compare banks 1 and 2: a difference points to one side. When the trim hits its limit — the threshold depends on the car, often around 20–25% — codes P0171/P0174 (lean) or P0172/P0175 (rich) appear.
Logging before and after the repair
Before the repair, save a report with the codes and freeze frames of all modules.
Record live data under the same conditions: warm idle, 2500 rpm, a test drive. Fuel trims, MAF, oxygen sensors, misfire counters, system voltage.
After the repair — the same set under the same conditions. The before-and-after comparison proves the repair to both you and the customer.
Save codes and freeze frames first; clear them after the repair.
Clearing resets the readiness monitors; permanent codes can’t be cleared with a scan tool.
STFT + LTFT within about ±10% is normal; plus means the module is adding fuel, minus means it’s taking fuel away.
Live data before and after the repair under the same conditions is proof of the repair.
Trucks — 24 V and J1939: the scan tool has to be rated for that.
Total fuel trim is +22% at warm idle and +4% at 2500 rpm. What is most likely?
A leaking injector
An unmetered air leak
High fuel pressure
At idle, airflow is low, so a leak has the biggest effect. At higher rpm its share drops and the trim gets smaller.
What happens if you clear the codes before diagnosing?
The freeze frames will be erased, the readiness monitors will reset, and the fault will come back
The fault will disappear for good
Nothing: the codes are stored in the scan tool
Clearing removes only the records, not the cause. Along with the codes, you lose the data on the conditions they appeared under.
All readiness monitors show “not ready”. What could that mean?
The car is completely fine
The OBD-II connector is faulty
The module was reset recently: codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected
An oxygen sensor is broken
After a reset, the module has to run its self-tests over a drive cycle. Until it does, the monitors are “not ready”.
Someone wants to plug a cheap 12 V adapter into a Howo truck’s connector. What’s the risk?
There’s no risk: it’s the same connector
The adapter will only show P codes
The adapter will work more slowly
The truck has a 24 V system — a 12 V adapter can burn out
A truck has 24 V on pin 16. The scan tool must be rated for that voltage and for the J1939 protocol.
Body and comfort electrics
How the body control module runs the locks, power windows and interior lighting, how comfort buses and module sleep work, and how to trace a fault from the module to the actuator.

In the past, the power window switch fed current to the motor directly. Now there’s almost always a module between the switch and the motor: it collects the switch signals, decides what to do and turns on the actuator — either itself or through another module over the bus.
Body control module
The names vary: BCM for most brands, BSI for Peugeot and Citroën, ETACS for Mitsubishi and on a number of Hyundai and Kia models.
Inputs: buttons, door, hood and trunk switches, the ignition switch, the key fob receiver. Outputs: lock actuators, interior lights, turn signals, window heating, horn.

The module is connected over buses to the instrument cluster, door modules, climate control and immobilizer. Many functions, such as speed-sensing auto door locking, are configured with a scan tool in manufacturer-specific mode.
It’s often located under the dashboard or in the footwell. Water from under the windshield or from clogged drains is a common cause of electrical “gremlins”.
Comfort buses

LIN is a slow single-wire bus for simple units, as in the lesson on data buses. The low-speed body CAN, usually up to 125 kbit/s, is fault-tolerant: if one wire is open or shorted, it can keep working on the other one, and a fault code stays in the modules’ memory. You won’t see 60 Ω between its wires, and the voltage levels are different — see the manual. Chevrolet and other GM vehicles may have the single-wire GMLAN body bus — pin 1 of the OBD-II connector.
Central locking and power windows

The lock actuator motor is reversible: the module switches polarity to lock or unlock. If one door doesn’t work, check the command at its connector, then the wires in the rubber boot between the door and the body, then the actuator.
Door switches affect a lot: interior lighting, the alarm, auto locking and modules going to sleep.

A power window with auto-up and anti-pinch protection knows the glass position from a Hall sensor in the motor. After the battery is disconnected or the motor or module is replaced, the “auto” mode is lost and the end positions need to be relearned. A typical procedure: lower the window all the way and keep holding the switch for a few more seconds, then raise it all the way and hold it again. The exact procedure and timing — per the manual.
Module sleep and wake-up

After the ignition is turned off and the car is locked, the modules exchange messages and go to sleep — usually after a few minutes; each car has its own timing. They’re woken by a door, the key fob, the ignition or a bus message. One module that doesn’t fall asleep keeps the bus awake and wakes the others — that’s a parasitic draw, as in the lesson on parasitic draw. Alarms connected to the bus can also keep modules from sleeping.
Tracing from the module to the actuator
Use the wiring diagram to work out which module receives the signal from the switch and which one drives the actuator.
In the module’s live data, check the input: does the button or door switch status change when pressed? If not, look in the switch and its wiring.
Activate the actuator with a scan tool test. If it works, the module output and the actuator are fine — look in the inputs, the settings or the conditions the function needs to work.
If it doesn’t work, measure the command at the actuator connector under load. Command present — the actuator or its ground is to blame. No command — the wiring from the module or the module output.
Before blaming the module, check its power supplies, grounds and bus communication.
There’s almost always a module between the switch and the actuator: check the input, the output and the wiring separately.
Low-speed body CAN can work on one wire; you won’t see 60 Ω on it.
After the battery is disconnected or the motor is replaced, the power window needs its end positions relearned — per the manual.
A module that doesn’t go to sleep keeps the bus awake and drains the battery.
The module’s live data and scan tool actuator tests save hours.
After the battery was replaced, the driver’s window stopped going up automatically. What should you do?
Replace the window motor
Replace the body control module
Relearn the end positions as described in the manual
Without power, the module forgot the window’s end positions and disabled auto-up. The relearn brings the function back.
When the lock button is pressed, its status in the BCM live data doesn’t change. Where should you look?
In the button and its wiring to the module
In the lock actuators
In the key fob receiver
In the engine CAN bus
The module doesn’t see the button press, so the signal is lost before it reaches the module: in the button, the connector or the wire.
The lock actuator works from the scan tool test, but not from the button. What does that mean?
The lock actuator is faulty
The module output and the actuator are fine — look in the input, the settings or the conditions the function needs to work
An open in the wire to the actuator
The scan tool test checked the output, the wiring and the actuator. What’s left is the part before the module and the module’s logic.
Why can the low-speed body CAN keep working with one wire open?
It’s a single-wire bus
That’s a fault, not a property of the bus
It has no resistors
It’s fault-tolerant: if one wire fails, it works on the other
That’s a property of this type of bus. That’s why an open often shows up not as a failure, but as a fault code in the modules’ memory.
Module-controlled and CAN-controlled lighting
How modules control bulbs with PWM and check that they’re working, why LEDs set fault codes, and what you need to know about xenon, LED headlights and headlight leveling.

On a modern car, the steering column stalk doesn’t turn on the headlights directly. It sends a command to the body control module — over wires or over the bus — and the bulbs are switched on by the body control module or a separate lighting module using power transistors. That brings new faults and new ways to track them down.
PWM and “smart” outputs

The module switches the bulb on through PWM. On some cars, this lets one filament work as both the tail light and the brake light, and the high beam at reduced brightness works as daytime running lights. A cold filament is switched on gradually, so bulbs last longer.
A multimeter on an output like this shows the average voltage, as in the PWM lesson. Use an oscilloscope or the module’s live data.
The output is short-circuit protected: when shorted, it shuts off and may not come back on until the module is restarted. Look for the short first, then suspect the module.
Bulb monitoring

The module measures the current through each output. If the current is below the threshold, the bulb is considered burnt out and a warning appears on the dash. Some modules also check the filament with the lights off — using short pulses that an incandescent bulb doesn’t notice.

An LED bulb draws only a fraction of the current, and the module sees an open: a fault code, the output shuts off, the turn signals blink twice as fast, and the test pulses make the LEDs flicker. The solutions are bulbs approved for that car, or reconfiguring the module with a scan tool if the manufacturer allows it. Load resistors that imitate a bulb get very hot: mount them only on metal, away from plastic and wires. And remember: the headlight must match the type of light source — an LED bulb in a halogen headlight blinds oncoming drivers.
The ballast ignites the arc with a pulse of around 20–25 thousand volts and then holds about 85 V AC across D1 and D2 bulbs and about 42 V across D3 and D4 bulbs.
Test by swapping in a known-good bulb or ballast, one at a time. Don’t switch on a ballast without a bulb.
Under international regulations, headlights with gas-discharge bulbs are fitted together with automatic leveling and headlight washers.

A xenon ballast can be lethal. Touch the bulb, ballast and connectors only with the lights off and the battery disconnected, after waiting for the capacitors to discharge for the time given in the manual. Don’t hold the bulb in your hand when it’s switched on, and don’t look at the arc.
LED headlights and their modules

The LEDs are powered by a driver — a module that maintains a constant current. It’s located in or on the headlight, often with a cooling fan, and communicates with the lighting module over LIN or CAN.
Typical faults: water and condensation, driver failure, overheating due to a stalled fan, individual sections burning out.
Repair is usually done by replacing modules. A new driver or headlight may need to be coded — per the manual.
Headlight leveling
Manual: a switch in the cabin sets the position, and the motors in the headlights adjust to it. Both headlights not working — the switch and its power supply; one — its motor and connector.

Automatic: the module lowers and raises the headlights based on ride height sensors on the suspension. After replacing a headlight, sensor or module, or after suspension work, a zero-position calibration is done with a scan tool: level ground, the car unloaded, tire pressures to spec. The exact procedure — per the manual.
The module switches bulbs through PWM and monitors their current; a multimeter on PWM shows the average.
An LED draws little current — the module thinks the bulb is burnt out.
Xenon: ignition pulse of around 20–25 kV; work only with the lights off and the battery disconnected.
LED headlight drivers and automatic leveling often need coding or calibration after parts are replaced — per the manual.
The module output shut off after a short — look for the short first.
After LED bulbs were fitted in the tail lights, a bulb warning appeared on the dash and the turn signals blink faster. Why?
LEDs draw little current, and the module thinks the bulb is burnt out
The tail light fuse has blown
The steering column stalk is faulty
The module judges a bulb by its current. The LED current is below the threshold, so the module reports an open circuit.
At the parking light output, a multimeter shows 4 V with 14 V in the system. What is this most likely?
An open wire
A faulty module output
PWM: the multimeter shows the average; look at the waveform with an oscilloscope
With PWM, a multimeter averages the pulses. An oscilloscope or the module’s live data will show the real picture.
How do you work safely on a xenon ballast?
Turn on the lights and check the connector with a probe
Only with the lights off and the battery disconnected, after waiting for the capacitors to discharge
Test the ballast on the bench without a bulb
Hold the bulb in your hand when switching on so you can see the arc
The ignition pulse is tens of thousands of volts. Only touch the components when they’re de-energized.
The ride height sensor for the automatic headlight leveling was replaced. What else needs to be done?
Nothing: the sensor will set itself up
Adjust the headlights by eye with the adjusting screws
Replace the leveling module too
Do a zero-position calibration with a scan tool as described in the manual
The new sensor sits slightly differently from the old one. Without calibration, the module will misread the body position and throw off the headlight aim.
Climate: heater, A/C, fans
How to check the heater blower and its resistor, the flap motors, the compressor clutch with the pressure sensor, and the radiator fan — without opening the A/C circuit.

Climate complaints are among the most common: the heater only blows on max, the modes won’t switch, the A/C doesn’t cool. Most of these faults are electrical, and you find them with a multimeter, a clamp meter and a scan tool. The refrigerant circuit itself is a job for an A/C station.
Heater blower and resistor

In a simple circuit, the speed is set by a resistor with several steps. On many cars, at top speed a relay or the switch sends current around the resistor. That’s why the complaint “only the top speed works” almost always means a burnt-out resistor or its thermal fuse.

With automatic climate control, there’s a regulator instead of a resistor — a power transistor or a PWM-controlled module on a heat sink in the airflow. The climate control unit sets the speed with a signal, and the regulator smoothly changes the voltage at the motor.
The blower fuse and relay.
The voltage right at the motor connector at each speed: it should rise from the first speed to the top one.

The motor current with a clamp meter — compare it with the spec in the manual or with a good car. A worn motor with tight bushings draws more current and burns out a new resistor, so when you replace the resistor, check the motor too.
Turn it by hand: if it’s stiff, noisy or has play, the motor needs replacing.
Flaps and flap motors

The blend, mode and recirculation flaps are moved by small motors. A simple motor with feedback has five wires: two for the motor and three for the potentiometer — 5 V reference, ground and the position signal. A bus motor has three wires: power, ground and a LIN or other bus line.

Symptoms: clicking behind the dash — stripped gear teeth or a stuck flap; the temperature or mode doesn’t change; a position fault in the climate control unit. Use the scan tool to compare the commanded and actual positions, then check power and signal at the motor connector. After replacing a flap motor or the control unit — and on some cars even after disconnecting the battery — a calibration is needed, with a scan tool or a button combination, strictly according to the manual. Don’t turn the flap by hand while the motor is connected.
Why the compressor won’t engage

The compressor clutch engages only when all the conditions are met: the button is pressed, the heater blower is running, the engine is running, the refrigerant pressure is within limits, the evaporator isn’t icing up, and the engine isn’t overheating. The decision is made by the climate control unit or the engine ECU, and the clutch relay receives the command. Conditions and thresholds — see the manual.
Scan tool: is there an A/C request, what pressure the sensor shows, and whether the unit commands the relay.
The clutch fuse and relay.

Voltage at the clutch connector when commanded — about battery voltage. If there’s voltage but the clutch doesn’t pull in, check the coil resistance (a few ohms, see the manual for the exact value) and the clutch air gap.
Pressure sensor: 5 V reference, ground, and a signal that rises with pressure. Compare the scan tool readings with the A/C station’s gauges. Older cars have a pressure switch instead of a sensor.

Low refrigerant — the sensor shows low pressure, and the unit won’t switch on the compressor. This is protection, not an electrical fault. Don’t jump the sensor and don’t power the clutch directly: without refrigerant, the compressor gets no lubrication and wears out quickly. A clutchless compressor with a control valve is checked by its control current on the scan tool.
Radiator fan

The ECU switches the fan on based on coolant temperature, and on many cars also when the A/C is running. Speeds are switched by a resistor, a relay or a PWM module. Testing: scan tool actuator test, voltage at the connector, current with a clamp meter. The current is high, so inspect the connector and the fuse socket for burn marks.

The A/C circuit is under pressure even with the engine off, and liquid refrigerant causes frostbite to skin and eyes. Don’t undo the lines or fittings and don’t remove the pressure sensor on a charged system — not every car has a valve under it. Charging, recovery and leak detection are done only at a station with the proper equipment.
“Only the top speed works” — almost always the heater resistor or its thermal fuse; check the motor current too.
Flap motors come with a potentiometer (5 wires) or as bus motors (3 wires); after replacement — calibration according to the manual.
The compressor engages only when all the conditions are met; low refrigerant pressure is protection, not a fault.
The radiator fan is checked with a scan tool test, the voltage at the connector and the current; inspect the connectors for burn marks.
Don’t open the refrigerant circuit — that’s for the A/C station only.
The heater blower works only at top speed. What is most likely faulty?
The fan motor
The heater resistor or its thermal fuse
The engine temperature sensor
On many cars, top speed bypasses the resistor. When the resistor goes open, that’s the only speed left.
A new heater resistor burned out a month after it was replaced. What should you check?
The blower motor current with a clamp meter and how freely the motor turns
The refrigerant pressure
The A/C pressure sensor
The radiator fan fuse
A worn motor draws more current and overheats the resistor. Unless the motor is replaced, the resistor will keep burning out.
The A/C won’t switch on, and the scan tool shows low refrigerant pressure. What should you do?
Jump the pressure sensor
Apply 12 V directly to the clutch
Send the car to an A/C station: the unit is keeping the compressor off for protection
With too little refrigerant, the compressor runs without lubrication. The unit protects it, and the station finds and fixes the leak.
What needs to be done after replacing a flap motor?
Turn the flap by hand all the way to the stop
Disconnect the battery for a day
Nothing, it will find its position by itself
Run a calibration with a scan tool or using the procedure in the manual
The unit needs to relearn the flap’s end positions. The calibration procedure depends on the car.
How an immobilizer and a smart key work, how to check power, ground and the antenna, and when the car needs to go to a key programming specialist.

The immobilizer won’t let the car start without “its own” key. When it fails, the engine won’t start or stalls right after starting, and the customer thinks the engine has broken down. An auto electrician has to tell a circuit fault from a key problem and know the limits of their job.
How it works
The transponder is a chip in the key head. It doesn’t need a battery: it’s powered by the antenna’s field.
The antenna coil is a ring around the ignition lock or near the start button. When the ignition is switched on, it creates a field, usually at around 125–134 kHz, and reads the key’s code.
The immobilizer unit compares the code with the stored ones. It can be a separate unit or built into the body control module, the instrument cluster or the ECU.
Link to the ECU: the immobilizer unit and the engine ECU exchange a code over K-line or CAN. Without permission, the ECU won’t allow injection or ignition, and on some cars the starter too.
Smart keys and emergency start

With keyless entry, antennas in the cabin and doors wake the key up with a low-frequency signal, the key replies over a radio link, and the unit checks that the key is inside the car. This needs a battery in the key.

If the battery is dead, almost all cars have an emergency start: you hold the key against the start button or put it in a special spot — the transponder inside works even without a battery. Where that spot is and how to start the car — see the car’s manual. The door is opened with the mechanical blade hidden in the key.
Symptoms of a fault
The immobilizer light flashes or stays on, or the dash shows “key not detected”.
The starter doesn’t crank even though the battery is charged.
The engine starts and stalls after 1–2 seconds.
The ECU has immobilizer codes or no communication with it — you’ll find code descriptions in the “Immobilizer” section of the “Error codes” tab.
What the auto electrician checks
Battery voltage: when it sags, the units lose communication and set key faults.
The spare key. If the spare works, the main key or its battery is faulty.
Interference: other chipped keys, fobs and tags on the same key ring, a phone near the start button. Try the key on its own, off the key ring.
The fuses for the immobilizer unit and the body control module.
Power and ground at the unit and antenna connectors according to the wiring diagram, under load — as in the lesson on the troubleshooting method.

The antenna: wires, connector, coil continuity; compare the resistance with the manual. An oscilloscope on the coil terminals will show bursts of a sine wave when the ignition is switched on — that means the unit is polling the key.
Key programming — only with documents

A new or additional key, or a replacement immobilizer unit or ECU, requires programming — pairing the keys and units to each other. It’s done by a specialist with the equipment, and only with the car’s documents: the registration certificate and the owner’s ID or a power of attorney. All the existing keys are often needed, and sometimes a PIN code from the dealer.

We don’t disable or bypass immobilizers, and we don’t program keys without the car’s documents. It’s anti-theft protection, and that kind of work helps car thieves. If a customer asks you to “disable the immobilizer”, refuse and offer to find and fix the cause of the fault.
The chain: transponder in the key — antenna coil — immobilizer unit — ECU permission.
A smart key with a dead battery calls for an emergency start — see the manual.
Battery, spare key, interference and fuses first, then power, ground and the antenna.
Key and unit programming — by a specialist, and only with the car’s documents.
The immobilizer is never bypassed or disabled.
The main key won’t start the car, but the spare starts it right away. Where should you look for the cause?
In the immobilizer unit
In the engine ECU
In the antenna coil
In the main key itself: transponder, battery, housing
The spare key works, which means the antenna, the unit and the ECU are fine. The main key is faulty.
The smart key battery is dead, and the car “doesn’t see” the key. What should you do?
Use the emergency start described in the manual, for example by holding the key against the start button
Disable the immobilizer
Replace the keyless entry unit
The transponder in the key works without a battery. That’s what the emergency start is for.
What will an oscilloscope show on the terminals of a good antenna when the ignition is switched on?
A steady 12 V
A flat zero
Bursts of a sine wave — the unit is polling the key
The unit briefly energizes the coil to read the transponder. A flat line is a reason to check power, ground and the connector.
Someone without the car’s documents asks you to program a key for them. What should you do?
Program it if the key is genuine
Refuse: programming only with the car’s documents and the owner’s ID
Disable the immobilizer so the key isn’t needed
Without documents, you can’t be sure the car belongs to the customer. The immobilizer is anti-theft protection.
Trucks: 24 V electrical system and the J1939 bus
Two batteries in series, the battery master switch, a 28 V alternator, SPN/FMI codes over the J1939 bus, Weichai and Cummins flash codes, and jump-starting 24 V correctly.

The principles are the same as in a passenger car, but the voltage is twice as high, the starter currents are higher, and diagnostics run over the J1939 bus. Here, that mainly means Shacman, Howo, FAW and KAMAZ trucks with Weichai and Cummins engines.
Two batteries and the battery master switch

24 V comes from two 12-volt batteries connected in series: the negative of the first to the positive of the second. The free positive goes to the starter and the electrical system, and the free negative goes through the battery master switch to the frame. At rest, the pair reads 24,8–25,8 V, and each battery 12,4–12,9 V.
Measure each battery separately. The pair may show a normal 25 V while one battery is weak and dragging the other one down.
Replace the batteries as a pair — same capacity and same age.
Don’t take 12 V from one battery for a radio or a fridge: the batteries get unbalanced — one is undercharged, the other overcharged. For 12-volt loads, a 24/12 V converter is fitted.

Don’t switch off the battery master switch with the engine running — it’s the same as removing a battery terminal while driving. After stopping the engine, wait the time given in the manual: the AdBlue system and the parking heater need to finish their purge.
28 V alternator

A truck alternator puts out about 28 V: with the engine running, the batteries usually read 27,5–28,5 V; see the manual for the exact values. The check is the same as in the lesson on the charging system: voltage under load, the drop on the positive cable and the ground, ripple. The currents are high, so a bad contact on the frame or a terminal causes heating and glitches faster here.
The J1939 bus and SPN/FMI codes

The engine, transmission, ABS and instrument cluster units communicate over a CAN bus using the J1939 standard. The bus physics is checked the same way as in the lesson on buses: with the vehicle powered down, about 60 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L. The diagnostic connector — a 9-pin round one or a 16-pin one like on passenger cars — depends on the vehicle.

A J1939 fault code is two numbers. SPN is the parameter number: what is faulty. FMI is the failure mode, from 0 to 31. For example, SPN 110 is coolant temperature, and FMI 4 is voltage below normal or shorted to ground. So we look for a short in the sensor circuit, not for the cause of overheating. You’ll find SPN and FMI descriptions in the “Error codes” tab. The scan tool shows some units’ faults as P-codes, like on passenger cars.
Flash codes without a scan tool

Many trucks with Weichai and Cummins engines have a diagnostic button or switch. With the ignition on, you press it, and the diagnostic lamp flashes out a fault code. Where the button is, how to count the flashes and what the code means — see the “Self-diagnosis” section. A flash code helps out on the road, but a scan tool gives the full picture.
Jump-starting 24 V
Only from another 24 V vehicle or a 24 V jump starter — to the free positive and negative of the pair, not to one battery.
Heavy-gauge cables with good clamps. Positive to positive first, then the donor’s negative to the frame of the vehicle being started.
Never jump-start a 12-volt passenger car from a truck: 24 V will destroy its electronics.

Removing AdBlue/SCR and EGR systems or fitting “emulators”, and tampering with the tachograph or speed limiter, are prohibited by law. We don’t do this kind of work and don’t recommend it. An SCR fault is tracked down like any other: power, ground, sensors, heating, fluid quality — more in the “AdBlue” section.

Parking heater repair
What Webasto, Eberspächer, Planar and Binar heaters are made of, how to read the codes, how to check the voltage during ignition, and why a heater won’t start.

In frosts down to −30…−40 °C, a parking heater is what lets a truck start and gives the driver a comfortable night in the cab. The most common ones are Webasto, Eberspächer, Planar (Avtoterm) and Binar, and there are plenty of Chinese “diesel air heaters” too. Air heaters warm the cab, coolant heaters warm the engine coolant. They are built in a similar way.
What it’s made of
Glow plug or glow pin — ignites the fuel at startup. On some models, the glow pin also works as the flame sensor.
Flame sensor (indicator) — confirms to the control unit that there’s combustion.
Overheat and temperature sensors — protect against overheating.
Fuel metering pump — an electromagnetic pump that delivers fuel in small portions. You can hear it clicking: the higher the output, the faster it clicks.
Combustion air blower — a motor with an impeller that supplies air for combustion.
Combustion chamber with an evaporator screen, and a heat exchanger; coolant heaters also have a circulation pump.
Control unit and a controller or timer.
How startup works

The unit checks the sensors and the voltage, purges the chamber, switches on the glow plug, then the metering pump and the blower. Once there’s a flame, the glow plug switches off and the heater goes into normal operation. If it doesn’t light — another attempt; after the failed attempts — a fault. When switched off, the heater purges and cools the chamber, so never cut its power with the battery master switch or by removing a terminal while it’s running or purging.
Diagnosing by codes

The code is shown on the controller or timer, and on simple controllers by the number of indicator flashes. Examples: on a Planar, 13 means it didn’t start after two attempts, 12 and 15 mean overvoltage and undervoltage; on a Webasto, F01 means no start, F02 means flame-out. Codes differ between models — you’ll find descriptions in the “Parking heater repair” section and in the model’s manual. Detailed parameters are shown by the manufacturer’s software through an adapter.
Voltage during startup

The glow plug draws a high current during ignition. A weak battery, thin wires, a corroded fuse holder or a poor ground — and the voltage sags: the unit logs a voltage fault or can’t ignite the fuel. Measure right at the heater’s power connector while the glow plug is on, and compare with the allowed range in the manual. Then check the voltage drop on the positive and on the ground.
Typical causes of faults
Fuel: summer diesel in the frost, a clogged filter or fuel pickup, air in the line, air leaks at the connections.
Carbon in the chamber and a clogged evaporator screen — cleaning with disassembly according to the manual. Carbon builds up from short runs at low output.
The exhaust pipe or air intake is blocked with snow, ice or dirt, or crushed.
Glow plug: wear or an open circuit — compare the resistance with the manual.
The metering pump doesn’t click — check the power at its connector; its delivery is checked with a measuring container according to the manual.
Overheating: on an air heater — the air outlets are blocked; on a coolant heater — air in the cooling system or the pump isn’t working.
Out of season, manufacturers advise running the heater once a month for about ten minutes — that way it cokes up less.

Carbon monoxide can’t be seen or heard, and it’s deadly. The heater exhaust is only ever routed outside; check the pipe for cracks and leaks. Don’t run the heater in a closed workshop bay without extraction. A cab where people sleep needs a carbon monoxide detector. Look for fuel leaks, don’t work near open flames, and keep a fire extinguisher at hand. At the filling station, the heater is switched off.

Hybrids and EVs: what an auto electrician may do
What makes the high-voltage system dangerous, how a certified specialist de-energizes it, and what an auto electrician without certification can do with the 12-volt system.

Hybrids and EVs come to an auto electrician with the usual complaints: won’t switch on, the battery drains, a warning light is on. Most of this work is on the 12-volt side. But the high-voltage system runs right next to it, and you need to know the boundary for certain.
Where the high voltage is

You can recognize the high-voltage system by its orange wires and connectors and by the warning labels. It’s the traction battery, the inverter, the electric motors, the cables between them, the electric A/C compressor and the high-voltage heater. The voltage is hundreds of volts: in hybrids it’s usually 100–300 V at the battery and more after the boost converter, and in EVs 400 or 800 V. This is lethal, and the inverter capacitors stay charged even after the system is switched off.
How a specialist de-energizes the system
This is theory — so you understand why it can’t be done without certification. The procedure always follows the manual for the specific car.
Switch the system off, exit READY mode, and move the smart key away from the car to the distance given in the manual.
Disconnect the negative of the 12-volt battery.
Wearing insulating gloves, remove the service plug — it breaks the traction battery circuit.
Wait for the capacitors to discharge — the time is given in the manual.
Use a meter of the right category to confirm there’s no voltage, and only then start work.

A certified specialist has been trained in high-voltage systems and works in protective equipment: insulating gloves of the right class, checked before every job, safety glasses or a face shield, insulated tools, an insulating mat, a fenced-off work area and a partner nearby.
What you can do without certification

The 12-volt battery. It doesn’t crank the engine, it only “wakes up” the system, so it’s small, often AGM, and is often located in the trunk or under a seat. If it’s flat, the car won’t go into READY. Charge it in AGM mode, and replace it with the same type.
Jump-starting — only at the points specified in the manual: many cars have a dedicated terminal under the hood.

The DC-DC converter replaces the alternator and charges the 12-volt battery from the traction battery. Check it only from the 12-volt side: in READY mode, the battery terminals should show charging voltage, usually about 13,5–14,5 V; see the manual for the exact value.
Ordinary 12-volt electrics: lights, power windows, locks, fuses, relays, power and ground to the control units, parasitic draw.
Scan tool diagnostics: codes and live battery data — read only.
What you must not do
Touch, disconnect or measure orange wires, connectors and components, even with the car switched off.
Remove the service plug, or open up the traction battery, the inverter or the electric compressor.
Recharge a hybrid’s A/C like a regular one: the electric compressor needs a special oil — only a shop that works with hybrids should do it.
Go near the high-voltage components of a car after a crash or a flood — that’s a job for a specialist.

In READY mode the car sits silently, but the engine can start by itself at any moment — for example, to charge the battery. Before working under the hood, switch the system off and remove the key. Don’t touch orange wires without certification: the high voltage in hybrids and EVs is life-threatening.
Orange wires and components mean high voltage: only a certified specialist in protective equipment may work on them.

Without certification — the 12-volt system, the 12-volt battery, the DC-DC converter from the 12-volt side, the scan tool.

The auto electrician trade: where to start
What tools you need at the start, how to set up your workspace, check in a car, explain the price and timeline to the customer, give a warranty and a report, and how to keep growing.
In auto electrics, accuracy and honesty are what count. The customer can’t see what you did inside the harness, so trust is built on a clear work process and a report.
Tools to start with
Multimeter: DC and AC voltage, resistance, continuity; with a safe category rating, good test leads and alligator clips.
A DC clamp meter — for parasitic draw, the starter and fans without breaking the circuit. A clamp meter that only measures AC is useless here.
An LED test light — safe for control unit circuits. An incandescent bulb is used as a load, but not in sensor and ECU circuits.
A 2–4 channel oscilloscope — for sensors, buses and ignition, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope.
A scan tool that supports the makes you work on — passenger cars and trucks.
A wiring repair kit: crimper, adhesive-lined heat shrink, soldering iron, terminals, terminal release tools, thin back-probes for measuring from the wire side of a connector.
A battery charger, a regulated power supply for working on control units, a jump starter.
Jumper wires with an inline fuse, a flashlight, electrical tape, cable ties.
Workspace

Good lighting, fender and seat covers, a fire extinguisher, tools kept in order. For bench work on control units — an antistatic mat and a wrist strap. Wiring diagrams and manuals at hand, on a tablet or a laptop.
How to check in a car
Write down the complaint in the customer’s own words and ask: when it started, under what conditions, whether it’s constant or intermittent, and what has already been repaired.
Inspect the car with the customer present: mileage, warning lights on the dash, damage, signs of previous wiring repairs. Take photos of the dash and the problem area.
Clarify any specifics: an alarm with remote start, aftermarket equipment, whether the customer has all the keys.
Fill out a work order: the car, the complaint, what’s been agreed, the timeline.
Price, timeline, warranty

Explain that diagnostics is a separate job: first we find the cause, then we give the cost of the repair. Intermittent faults take time — say so up front. Agree on every additional job with the customer before starting it. Discuss the warranty on labor and parts in advance and write down its terms.
“Before/after” photos and a report

A photo of a corroded connector or a chafed wire is the best explanation for a customer. Keep the report short: the complaint, what you found and which measurements confirmed it, what you did and replaced, what you recommend. Give the old parts back to the customer.
How to keep learning
Read the wiring diagram of every car you work on — it’s the key skill.
Keep a case log: make, complaint, cause, measurements. In a year, it will be your own knowledge base.
Measure healthy cars and write down the values — they’ll come in handy for comparison.
Learn from equipment manufacturers and on professional courses, and work through difficult cases with experienced technicians.
Go from simple to complex: wiring, buses, ECUs, trucks. High-voltage systems — only after training and certification.
