Service culture: taking care of the customer’s car
How to dress, what to cover the car with and how to behave inside it, so the customer sees a professional and not a backyard garage job.

A customer judges the work not only by whether the car runs again. They see the condition the car comes back in: whether there are scratches on the fender, marks on the steering wheel and seat, whether the interior is tidy. Being careful costs almost nothing, but it’s exactly what sets a professional apart from a backyard garage and brings customers back — and brings in referrals.
Clothes that won’t damage the car

Scratches in the paint are most often left not by tools but by the technician: a belt buckle, rivets and metal buttons on jeans, a jacket zipper — when you lean over a fender or lie across a door sill.
Work overalls or a jacket with covered buttons and plastic fasteners.
No belt with a metal buckle, no metal buttons or rivets on the front.
Take off watches, rings and bracelets: they scratch the paint and the interior plastic.
Clean hands or nitrile gloves — especially before getting into the car.
A technician dresses so that nothing on them can damage the car: no belts with metal buckles and no metal buttons.
Fender covers — against scratches, not dirt

A fender cover isn’t there to keep you from getting dirty on the car, but to keep you from scratching it. You lean on the fender with your hands, elbows and stomach, and you put test leads and wires down next to you. A soft cover with a non-slip backing or magnets takes all of that.
Covers on both fenders, and if you’re working near the bumper — on the bumper too.
Don’t put tools on the body, roof or hood — only on an organizer mat or a tool cart.
Before laying down a cover, brush the sand off the fender: under the cover, it acts like sandpaper.
A drop of battery acid leaves a mark on the paint: wash it off with water right away.
Seat, steering wheel and floor covers

A good technician puts a cover on the seat not because they’re dirty, but because they care about the customer’s car. A separate steering wheel cover and a floor mat are things the customer notices right away when they get behind the wheel after the repair. These are usually inexpensive disposable plastic covers for the seat, steering wheel and gear lever, and a paper floor mat.
Covers on the seat and a separate one on the steering wheel show care for the customer’s car. That’s exactly the plus that sets you apart from a backyard garage.
Checking in and handing back the car
At check-in, walk around the car with the customer and photograph it: existing chips and scratches won’t become a matter of dispute later.
Remember the position of the seat, mirrors and steering wheel; if you had to move them, put them back as they were.
If you need to disconnect the battery, warn the customer: the clock, radio and power window settings may reset. After the work, restore them according to the manual.
Don’t smoke in the car, don’t use the customer’s things, and don’t take their charger or phone without asking.
Before handing the car back, remove the covers with the customer present, wipe the steering wheel, handles and gear lever, and clear tools and trash out of the interior and the engine bay.
Show the removed parts and explain what was done: the old parts belong to the customer.

The technician’s clothes — no metal buckles, buttons or rivets; take off watches and rings.

ECU repair

For those who have completed the auto electrician course and want to repair the control modules themselves: how an ECU is built, the workbench, connecting on the bench, troubleshooting, soldering, module memory and handing the unit back to the customer.
What’s inside an ECU

What sections make up a control module’s circuit board — the power supply and 5 V regulator, the processor and crystal, memory, input circuits, output stages, bus transceivers — and how they connect to the connector.

This level is for those who already know how to check a module’s power and grounds on the car. Now we take the cover off: to repair a module rather than replace it, you need to know what sections are on the board and what usually fails in them.
What a module is made of

An ECU — electronic control unit — is a small computer: a housing, a multilayer printed circuit board and a connector. It receives sensor signals, does the calculations its program sets out and switches on the actuators. There are six main sections: the power supply, the processor with its crystal, memory, input circuits, output stages and bus transceivers.
Power supply and 5 V regulator

+30, +15 and power from the main relay come in through the connector. First comes protection: diodes against reverse polarity and voltage spikes, chokes and filter capacitors. Then the regulator — a chip that turns the vehicle’s 12–14 V into a steady 5 V. It often has several outputs: one for the processor and a separate 5 V reference for the sensors; many modules also have 3.3 V. If the 5 V reference is shorted in the car’s wiring, the regulator goes into protection or burns out, and codes appear for several sensors at once. That’s why you look for a short in the wiring first.
Processor, crystal and memory

The processor, or microcontroller, is the module’s “brain” and usually the largest chip: a package with pins on all four sides (QFP) or with solder balls underneath (BGA). Inside are the computing core, an ADC that converts the sensor voltage into a number, and timers.
The crystal sets the processor’s clock frequency, like a metronome. It’s a small metal or ceramic package next to the processor. No clock — the processor stops, and there’s no communication.
Flash holds the program and calibrations, that is, the tables used to calculate injection and ignition. In modern modules it’s most often inside the processor; in older ones it’s a separate chip.

EEPROM holds data that changes: adaptations, the VIN, immobilizer data. It’s often a small 8-pin chip; in newer modules it’s an area of the processor’s memory. More on this in the lesson on module memory.
Sensor input circuits

A sensor signal reaches the processor through an input circuit: resistors, filter capacitors and protection diodes cut out interference and bring the signal to the right level. The temperature sensor input is pulled up to 5 V through a resistor — that’s why you see about 5 V with the sensor disconnected, and the scan tool shows a very low temperature. A signal conditioner turns the inductive crankshaft sensor’s signal into square pulses. If 12 V gets onto the signal wire, the input resistor or protection diode usually burns out, and the module “doesn’t see” the sensor even though the wiring is fine.
Output stages

A processor output delivers only milliamps, so the load is switched on by an output stage, or driver — a power transistor or a multi-channel chip. It usually switches the load’s negative to ground, as in the lesson on actuators. Coils without a built-in igniter are driven by ignition transistors, and flap motors by H-bridge drivers that reverse polarity. Drivers get hot and are mounted on a heat sink. Many of them detect an open circuit, a short and overheating on their own — that’s where codes like “open circuit” or “short to positive” come from. More detail in the lesson on output stages.
Bus transceivers

The processor “talks” in logic signals, while the wiring carries a CAN bus or a K-line. The translation is done by a transceiver — usually a small 8-pin chip near the connector. It’s the first to take spikes and shorts on the bus, so a burnt-out transceiver is one of the reasons a module stays silent even with good power.
How the board is wired to the connector
The connector is soldered or press-fit into the board. Power and grounds run along wide traces, often through several parallel pins. Every module has its own pin numbers.

The board is multilayer: traces pass from layer to layer through vias — plated holes in the board. A break inside can’t be seen; you find it with a continuity test from the connector pin to the component.
There are power grounds — for the drivers — and signal grounds — for the sensors. They may be routed separately, so on the car you check all the grounds.
Check the fuses first. Before you remove a module and open it up, spend five minutes on the fuses for its power feeds and for the main relay.

Chips don’t tolerate static: a discharge you won’t even feel can damage a processor input or a transceiver. Hold the board by its edges, don’t touch the pins and traces with your fingers, and work with an antistatic wrist strap — more in the lesson on the workbench.
Power goes through the protection to the 5 V regulator, which supplies the processor, memory and sensors.
Without a working crystal the processor won’t run; the program is in flash, and adaptations and immobilizer data are in EEPROM or in the processor’s memory.
Input circuits protect the processor, drivers switch the loads, and the transceiver connects the module to the bus.
Each connector pin goes to its own section; a break inside the board is found with a continuity test.

Workbench and safety

What you need to repair modules on the bench — antistatic protection, a bench power supply with current limiting, a soldering station, a hot-air station, magnification and cleaning — what you must never do, and how to remove and install a module on the car.

Most “finished-off” modules are ruined not by the original fault but by careless repair: static, reverse polarity, an accidental short with a probe. A good workbench isn’t about expensive equipment — it’s about a routine that keeps you from making mistakes.
Antistatic protection

An antistatic wrist strap on your wrist, with its lead going to a ground point. The lead has a resistor of about 1 MΩ in it: the charge drains off gradually, and it protects you if you accidentally touch a live voltage.
An antistatic mat on the bench — connected to the same ground point. Put the module and the board only on the mat.
Store and transport boards in antistatic bags. Ordinary polyethylene, foam and synthetics build up charge.
In winter, when the heating is on, the indoor air is dry and there’s more static — the wrist strap is especially important.
Power on the bench

A battery is no good for the bench: if something goes wrong, it delivers hundreds of amps, and a thin trace burns out instantly. You need a bench power supply with adjustable voltage and current limiting, up to 30 V — so it can also handle 24 V truck modules. Set the voltage, for example 13.5 V for a passenger car module, and a low current limit for the first power-up — 0.5–1 A. If there’s a short on the board, the power supply goes into current limiting, and you’ll see it on the ammeter, not by the smoke. Connect the module with the power supply output turned off.
Soldering, magnification and cleaning
A soldering station with temperature control, fine tips and grounding. A soldering iron without temperature control isn’t suitable for circuit boards.
A hot-air station with temperature and airflow control — for chips and connectors. Between jobs, keep the handpiece only on its stand.
Electronics flux, solder and desoldering braid. Acid flux on a board is unacceptable: it keeps eating away at the traces.
An illuminated magnifier or a microscope: cracked solder joints, a hair-thin strand of solder between pins or a darkened resistor can only be seen under magnification.
Isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush — for cleaning off flux and dirt. Soldering is covered in the lesson on soldering, cleaning and drying in the lesson on moisture and corrosion.
What you must never do
Reverse polarity. Mixing up positive and negative is one of the common reasons a module dies. The red lead is positive, the black one is negative; check once more before switching on.
Probing chip pins with power on. A slipping probe shorts adjacent pins — and a second fault is added to the first. Measure with a fine probe on resistor or capacitor leads, or at test points.
Applying voltage “just to check”. 12 V on an input designed for 5 V burns out the input circuit.
Soldering and heating the board with power on. Before soldering, disconnect the power supply and the diagnostic adapter.
Repairing without a memory backup. Heating, soldering or a power mistake can corrupt the data. First read and save the module’s memory — we’ll show how in the lesson on module memory.

The power supply, soldering station and hot-air station run on 220 V — keep an eye on the condition of the cords. The hot-air nozzle and the soldering tip heat up to hundreds of degrees. Work in a ventilated area: flux fumes are harmful, and isopropyl alcohol ignites easily — keep it away from the hot-air station and the soldering iron.
How to remove and install a module on the car
Read the codes in all modules and save the scan tool report — so you’ll have something to compare against later.
Turn off the ignition and wait: the module keeps the main relay on for a while, as in the lesson on ECU power and grounds.
Disconnect the battery negative. Check the manual beforehand for what you’ll need after disconnecting it: the radio code, power window relearn and so on.
Discharge static by touching body ground, release the lock and pull the connector off straight, without tilting it. Don’t pull on the wires.
Inspect the connector: water, green corrosion, backed-out terminals. Take photos. Cover the harness connector with a bag, and don’t wash the engine bay in the meantime.
In winter, don’t put a module that’s just come in from the cold straight onto the bench: let it warm up in a sealed bag, otherwise condensation will form on the board.
Installation is the reverse: the connector until the lock clicks, the seal in place, then the battery negative. Turn on the ignition and check communication and codes.
The wrist strap and the mat share one ground; boards go in antistatic bags.
On the bench, use a bench power supply with current limiting, not a battery.
Never: reverse polarity, probing pins with power on, soldering with power on, or repairing without a memory backup.
The module is removed with the ignition off and the battery negative disconnected, the connector is protected from moisture, and in winter the module is warmed up in a sealed bag.
Why is a module on the bench powered from a bench power supply rather than a battery?
A battery’s voltage is too low
In a short, the power supply limits the current, while a battery delivers hundreds of amps and burns the traces
The scan tool requires it
Current limiting turns a short from a fire into a number on the ammeter.
What needs to be done before soldering and heating the board?
Read and save the module’s memory, then disconnect the power
Turn on the ignition so the module doesn’t go to sleep
Wipe the board with a damp cloth
Nothing, if the board is clean
Heating and soldering can corrupt the data, and with power on you can fry the board. Backup first, then repair with the power off.
In what order is a module removed from the car?
Unplug the connector, then turn off the ignition
Disconnect the battery negative with the engine running
Read the codes, turn off the ignition, wait, disconnect the battery negative and discharge static — and only then unplug the connector
This way the module has time to go to sleep and save its data, and the connector comes off with no voltage and no static.
A module has been brought in from the winter cold. What should you do?
Open it right away and start testing
Heat it with the hot-air station until it’s hot
Put it on a heating radiator
Let it warm up in a sealed bag
Condensation forms on a cold board in a warm room. In a sealed bag the module warms up dry.
Connecting a module on the bench

How to power a module on the bench: +30, +15, all grounds, the main relay and output power, the diagnostic line to the adapter, 12 and 24 V — and how to tell from the current whether the module has woken up.

On the bench, you test the module and read its codes and memory without the car. The goal is to give it everything it gets in the car: power, grounds and communication with the diagnostic adapter. A mistake in a single wire is costly here, so the diagram and checks come first, and power-up comes after.
Power feeds and grounds
+30 — constant positive, from the bench power supply through a fuse.
+15 — ignition; for the module it’s the “wake up” command. Feed it through a separate switch: that way you turn the “ignition” on and off without touching the other wires.
All grounds together — to the power supply negative. A single unconnected ground is a common reason a module won’t wake up or behaves strangely.

Voltage. Passenger cars are 12 V; on the bench you supply about 12–14 V, for example 13.5 V. Trucks and heavy equipment — Shacman, Howo, FAW, KAMAZ — are 24 V, and they get 24–28 V. A passenger car module can burn out on 24 V, and a truck module may not wake up on 12 V. Check the module’s voltage in the documentation before switching on.
Main relay and output power

In the car, once the module gets +15, it switches on the main relay itself, and power comes back from contact 87 into the module and goes to the loads — as in the lesson on ECU power and grounds. Many modules won’t communicate without this power. On the bench there are two ways. The first is a real relay: contact 30 and coil terminal 86 to positive, terminal 85 to the module pin that controls the relay. The module will switch the relay on itself, and you’ll test that output at the same time. The second is to apply positive to the “power from relay” pins together with +15: simpler, but the relay control stays untested. Power the load simulators — covered in the lesson on output stages — from contact 87.
Diagnostic line
The module’s CAN-H and CAN-L go to pins 6 and 14 of the OBD-II connector the adapter plugs into. K-line goes to pin 7.
Power the adapter from the same power supply: pin 16 is positive, 4 and 5 are ground. A common ground for the module and the adapter is a must.

A CAN bus needs termination resistors, as in the lesson on digital buses. If the module has its own resistor, you’ll read about 120 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L with the module unpowered; if the resistance is very high, fit an external 120 Ω resistor between them.
Cars up to the late 2000s, including many right-hand-drive Japanese cars, often use K-line or the manufacturer’s own protocol. Which line a module has — check the documentation.
Where to get the pinout
This lesson deliberately has no pin numbers: every module has its own, even similar modules from the same manufacturer on different cars. Take the pinout and connection diagram from trusted sources:
Autodata and HaynesPro (WorkshopData) — diagrams and pinouts by make and engine.
The carmaker’s official documentation — for example, ELSA for Volkswagen, TIS for Toyota.
The manual for your programmer or test bench: equipment makers provide connection diagrams for specific modules.

Before the first power-up, check the diagram against the module: the number of pins, the markings on the housing. On many modules the ground pins read almost a dead short to each other — a handy way to confirm you’ve found them.

Only take pinouts from trusted sources — Autodata, HaynesPro, the manufacturer’s documentation. Diagrams from forums and random pictures are often wrong, and a mistake on a single pin can fry the module.
Current draw: awake or not

The power supply’s ammeter is your first instrument. Current limit for the first power-up — 0.5–1 A. You apply +30 — the current is almost zero, a few milliamps: the module is asleep and holding its memory. You switch on +15 — the current steps up and holds steady: the module has woken up, and the main relay often clicks. You switch off +15 — the module holds the relay for a while and goes to sleep. How much an awake module draws depends on the model; use an identical good module or the test bench data as a reference.

The current doesn’t change when +15 is switched on — the module hasn’t woken up. Check +15 and the grounds along the bench wiring, then the power supply on the board — this is covered in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate.
The current hits the limit right away — there’s a short inside. Turn off the power and don’t raise the limit “to get it going”: whatever is still intact will burn out.
The module keeps waking up and resetting — a bad contact in the bench wiring, a voltage sag or a power supply fault on the board.
Normal current but no communication — check the diagnostic line, the common ground, the 120 Ω resistor, the adapter power and the module selected in the scan tool.

Connect and disconnect the wires to the module only with the power supply output turned off. Check the polarity and voltage before switching on. Don’t apply positive to pins whose purpose you don’t know, and don’t short pins together “just to see”.
On the bench: +30, +15 through a switch, all grounds together, power from the main relay, and the diagnostic line with a common ground.
Pinouts only from trusted sources: Autodata, HaynesPro, the manufacturer’s documentation, the test bench manual.
Passenger car modules are 12 V, truck modules are 24 V; check the voltage before switching on.
Current: almost zero — asleep; a steady step after +15 — awake; hits the limit — a short.
Where should you get a module’s pinout for connecting it on the bench?
From a picture on an internet forum
From Autodata, HaynesPro, the manufacturer’s documentation or the test bench manual
From memory, going by a similar module from another car
A mistake on a single pin can fry the module. Even similar modules on different cars have different pinouts.
You apply +30 — the current is almost zero. You switch on +15 — the current doesn’t change. What does that mean?
The module hasn’t woken up: check +15, the grounds and the power supply on the board
The module is fine and working
You need to raise the current limit to the maximum
An injector has burned out
An awake module draws noticeably more current. No step — no +15, no ground or no power on the board.
You’re connecting a module from a Shacman truck on the bench. What’s important to check before switching on?
That 12 V is being supplied — it’s safer
Nothing, all modules are the same
That 36 V is being supplied — to have some headroom
What voltage the module is designed for: trucks are usually 24 V
Truck modules are designed for 24 V, passenger car modules for 12 V. The voltage is checked against the documentation before switching on.
The awake module’s current is normal, but the scan tool can’t see it over CAN. What should you check?
Replace the processor
Raise the voltage to 18 V
The CAN-H and CAN-L connections, the common ground with the adapter and the 120 Ω resistor
The module is working, so the problem is in the communication line: the bus wires, the adapter ground or the termination resistor.
A module that won’t communicate

The order of checks when the scan tool can’t see a module: power and grounds at the connector, current draw, the 5 V regulator, the crystal, the CAN transceiver, traces and vias, signs of moisture — and how to tell a module fault from a fault in the car’s wiring.

“No communication with the module” is a common complaint and a common diagnostic mistake: the module gets removed and taken in for repair, but it’s fine — power or the bus just isn’t reaching it. So the order is: the car first, then the bench.
The car first

See which modules you have communication with. None at all — look for a common cause: power and ground at the OBD connector (16 is positive, 4 and 5 are ground), the bus as a whole, or a module that’s “jamming” the bus, as in the lesson on digital buses. No communication with just one — check that one.

Power and grounds at the module connector: +30, +15, power from the main relay and all grounds — from the wire side, under load, as in the lesson on ECU power and grounds. Which pin is which — only from a pinout from a trusted source.
Bus: with the car unpowered, about 60 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L; with the ignition on, about 2.5 V on each wire at the module connector. K-line at rest — about battery voltage.
The module connector terminals: water, corrosion, spread or backed-out terminals — as in the lesson on wiring repair.
Everything is normal but there’s still no communication — the module is removed and tested on the bench.
Check the fuses first. If a module is silent, the first thing to look at is the fuses for its power feeds and for the main relay.
On the bench: from simple to complex

Connect the module using a verified diagram, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. Each next step only makes sense if the previous one is normal: there’s no point measuring the crystal while the processor has no power.

Current draw. It doesn’t rise when +15 is switched on — the module hasn’t woken up. It hits the limit right away — a short in the power circuit: don’t power it up any further, look for the shorted component.
Power on the board. +30, +15 and power from the relay must get from the connector pins to the board — check after the protection components and at the regulator input.

5 V regulator. With +15 on, measure at its output or at the capacitors near the processor relative to board ground: it should be a steady 5 V. If the module has 3.3 V, check that too. No voltage, or it “wanders” — the power supply chip is faulty or something is loading its output.

Crystal. With an oscilloscope on its pins — a clean sine wave at a frequency that’s usually marked on the package. Set the probe to x10: an x1 probe loads the crystal more and can stop the oscillation. No oscillation — the crystal, the capacitors next to it or the processor.

CAN transceiver. On an awake module, CAN-H and CAN-L read about 2.5 V each. On an unpowered module, the resistance from each line to ground is high, not a few ohms. Almost zero — the transceiver or a protection component at the bus input is shorted.
Traces and vias. Do a continuity test from the connector pin to the component: power — to the regulator, CAN — to the transceiver, ground — to board ground.
Signs of moisture: white or green deposits, darkened areas, corroded pins, especially near the connector. What to do about them — in the lesson on moisture and corrosion.

Measurements on a powered board — only with fine probes and with your hand braced. A slipping probe will short 12 V onto a neighboring 5 V circuit — and you’ll lose the processor. The oscilloscope ground clip goes only to board ground. Don’t leave jumpers or loose wires on a powered board.
Symptoms and likely causes
Current almost zero with +15 on — power isn’t reaching the board: a broken trace, a protection component at the input, or the regulator won’t start.
Current hits the limit — a short in the power circuit: a protection diode, a capacitor, a driver, the power supply chip.

Current is normal, 5 V is present, the crystal is running, but there’s no communication — the transceiver, the bus traces, water near the connector, or a corrupted program in memory; more on that in the lesson on module memory.
Communication comes and goes — cracked solder joints, corrosion, a bad contact. Check how the module reacts to light tapping and to heating.
Module or wiring

The bench gives the final answer. If the module comes online on the bench with correct power — look in the car: power, grounds, bus, connector. If it won’t communicate on the bench, while power, grounds and the bus at the connector in the car are fine — the module is faulty. It also happens that the module works on the bench but not in the car — because of a spread terminal in the harness connector.

On trucks with Weichai and Cummins engines, the engine ECU is often mounted right on the engine. Vibration, heat, frost and pressure-washing the engine hit both the connector and the board, so on these trucks inspecting the connector is the first step.
The car first: fuses, power and grounds at the connector, the bus, the terminals — and only then does the module go on the bench.
On the bench, in order: current, power on the board, 5 V, crystal, transceiver, traces, signs of moisture.
The crystal is measured with an x10 probe; on a powered board, work with a fine probe and your hand braced.
Works on the bench but not in the car — look in the wiring and the harness connector.
The scan tool can’t see any module in the car. Where do you start?
Remove the engine ECU and take it to the bench
Replace the transceiver in the engine ECU
With what they all share: fuses, power and ground at the OBD connector, the bus as a whole
When all the modules are silent, the cause is a common one. A single module rarely explains losing communication with all of them.
On the bench the current is normal, 5 V is present, there’s a sine wave on the crystal, but no CAN communication. What do you check next?
The CAN transceiver and the traces from it to the connector
The current draw, once again
Raise the supply voltage to 24 V
Replace the crystal
Power and clock are fine, which means the processor is running. The next section on the way to the bus is the transceiver and its traces.
Why is the crystal checked with an oscilloscope probe set to x10?
It shows the current better
x1 mode is prohibited for boards
So the frequency reads 10 times higher
An x1 probe loads the crystal more and can stop the oscillation
An x10 probe has lower capacitance, so it barely affects the oscillator and doesn’t distort the picture.
The module communicates on the bench but not in the car. Where should you look?
In the car: power, grounds, the bus and the harness connector terminals
A module that works on the bench tells you it’s missing something in the car: power, ground, the bus or a contact in the connector.
Output stages: why they burn out and how to test them
Why injector, coil, relay and motor drivers burn out, how to test a module output with a load simulator and an oscilloscope, and why the cause in the car’s wiring has to be fixed first.

An output stage, or driver, is a transistor or chip through which the module switches on a load: an injector, a coil, a relay, a flap motor. It’s rated for its load’s current with a small margin. With a short in the wiring, the current rises several times over, and the driver fails: modern drivers do have short-circuit protection, but it isn’t all-powerful. After the failure, the module can’t switch on the injector or relay, or sometimes, on the contrary, keeps them on all the time.
Why outputs burn out

The control wire shorted to positive. The driver switches the wire to ground, but the wire is already connected to positive — only the wiring limits the current. Typical cases: a chafed injector harness or a wire pinched against a positive wire.
A faulty load: shorted turns in an injector, a valve or a relay coil.
The wrong load: low-impedance injectors instead of high-impedance ones, a relay with a different coil, add-on equipment on the module output.
A broken-down ignition coil, or checking for spark “to ground” without a spark tester, as in the lesson on actuators.
Mistakes during work: reversed polarity when jump-starting, welding without disconnecting the module, a test lamp on the module pins.
On trucks, the harnesses are long and run along the frame — check the places where they touch the frame and brackets.

The main rule: first find and fix the cause in the car’s wiring. A new driver on the same wiring with the same short will burn out again — sometimes within the first seconds after starting. The customer pays twice, and you lose the part, your time and their trust.
Wiring and load first
Read the codes: on which outputs the module itself sees an open, a short to ground or a short to positive. You’ll find code descriptions in the “Error codes” tab.

Turn off the ignition, disconnect the battery negative and the module connector. From the harness side, measure the resistance of the load — injector, coil, relay. Spec — per the manual; compare identical circuits with each other.
Disconnect the load and check the control wire for a short to ground and to positive: the resistance should be high. Wiggle the harness — a chafed spot often shorts only when it moves.
Find the damage and repair the wiring, as in the lesson on wiring repair. Only after that — repair or install the module.
Check the fuses first. A blown fuse in the injector or coil circuit is a clue: there was a short somewhere, and it may be exactly what finished off the module output.
Testing with a load simulator

On the bench, a load simulator is connected to the output instead of an injector or relay. If the output switches the negative, the simulator’s positive is taken from contact 87 of the main relay or from the power supply, and its negative from the module output; if the output switches the positive, the simulator is connected between the output and ground. When the output switches on, the simulator lights up.
An LED with a resistor of about 1 kΩ for 12 V (about 2.2 kΩ for 24 V) draws about 10 mA: it’s safe for any output and shows the pulses by blinking.

A small bulb tests the output under load: a “tired” driver may light an LED but not hold a bulb. The bulb’s current must be no higher than this output’s factory load; a 21 W test lamp can burn out a weak output.
The most accurate simulator is the factory load itself: a real injector or relay.

To make the module switch an output on, you need an actuator test with the scan tool or a simulated crankshaft signal on the test bench: without a rotation signal, many modules won’t switch the injectors and coils on.
Oscilloscope on the output

Probe on the module output with the factory load connected, ground clip on module ground. On a good output that switches the negative: while it’s off — supply voltage, about 12–14 V; when it switches on — a drop almost to zero; on an injector, when it switches off — an inductive spike, as in the oscilloscope lesson.
Under the factory load, the drop isn’t almost to zero but noticeably higher — a volt or more: the driver is “tired”, it runs hot and will soon fail.
No pulses, supply voltage on the output all the time — the driver is open, or the module hasn’t received the command: no rotation signal, or the test isn’t running.
The output reads almost zero all the time, even when it should be off — the driver is shorted.
The spike on one channel is noticeably lower than on the neighboring ones — check the load winding and that driver’s protection circuit.

A burnt-out driver is replaced with an identical part or a full equivalent; if the output was part of a multi-channel chip, the chip is replaced. Check the neighboring components too: resistors, protection diodes, the trace — a short often damages them as well. Soldering is covered in the lesson on soldering and replacing components, testing after repair in the lesson on handing the unit back to the customer.

A module with a shorted injector output must not be installed on the car: the injector will pour fuel continuously — flooded spark plugs, oil washed off the cylinder walls and, with a large amount of fuel, hydrolock. Gasoline direct injection and Common Rail diesel injector outputs operate at voltages from tens to hundreds of volts: LEDs and bulbs are never connected to them; they’re tested only with equipment designed for this.
A driver burns out from a short in the wiring or the wrong load — first find and fix the cause in the car.
On the bench, an output is tested with an LED and a resistor of about 1 kΩ, a small bulb whose current matches the factory load, or the factory load itself.
Oscilloscope: a good output drops almost to zero, a “tired” one doesn’t, a shorted one is always near zero.
Direct injection and Common Rail mean high voltage: bulbs and LEDs are never connected to them.
After the injector driver was replaced, the module was installed on the car, and a minute later the output burned out again. What was the main mistake?
The driver was too powerful
The short in the car’s wiring wasn’t found and fixed
The codes weren’t cleared after the repair
The short was still there — and the new driver burned out just like the old one. Wiring first, then the module.
What can you safely use to test a module output on the bench?
A 21 W test lamp
Apply 12 V directly to the output
An LED with a resistor of about 1 kΩ from positive to the output
An ohmmeter with the module powered on
An LED with a resistor draws about 10 mA — that’s safe for any output and easy to see.
Under the factory load, when the output switches on, the voltage drops not almost to zero but to a few volts. What does that mean?
The driver is “tired”: it runs hot and will soon fail
That’s normal for any output
The load has burned out
A good driver pulls the output almost to zero. A few volts left over is a sign of a worn transistor.
On the bench, a good module won’t switch the injectors on. Why does this happen?
Injectors never work on the bench
The power supply is too powerful
The antistatic wrist strap is interfering
Without a crankshaft rotation signal, many modules won’t switch the injectors on
The module only injects fuel when it sees rotation. On the bench you need a scan tool test or a simulated crankshaft signal.
Moisture, corrosion and vibration
How water gets into a module, how to clean and dry the board, restore eaten-away traces, find solder cracks caused by vibration and protect the board with conformal coating after the repair.

Water and vibration are the most common reasons a once-healthy module ends up on the bench. Corrosion eats away a trace over years, and a cracked solder joint causes a fault only over bumps or in freezing weather. Such modules can be repaired if you find all the damage and eliminate the cause.
How water gets into a module
Through a dried-out or damaged housing or connector seal.
Along the wires: water runs into the harness and wicks along the strands under the insulation all the way to the connector.
From outside: a clogged drain under the windshield, a leak into the cabin, pressure-washing the engine, and on trucks, spray with salt and de-icing chemicals.
Condensation: in winter a frozen module goes into a warm service bay, and moist air gets in through a poorly sealed housing and settles on the cold board.

With power on, moisture between pins at different voltages acts as an electrolyte: metal dissolves, and corrosion and thin conductive “bridges” grow. That’s why you must never power up a wet module “to check it” — you’ll only speed up the damage.
Inspection, cleaning and drying
Photograph the board before you start work — for the customer report.

Inspect both sides under a magnifier or microscope: green or white deposits, darkened traces, rusty connector pins, bulging or leaking electrolytic capacitors — their electrolyte causes corrosion on its own. Look from the side under chip packages: corrosion often hides there.

Clean off the deposits with isopropyl alcohol of 99% purity or higher and a soft brush. Heavy corrosion is removed with a stiff brush or a fiberglass pen, without scraping off the solder mask — the protective layer over the traces.
Leaking capacitors and parts with eaten-away leads are replaced — that’s covered in the next lesson.

An ultrasonic cleaner gets under components better than a brush, but crystals, built-in pressure and acceleration sensors and parts with membranes can be damaged by it. Ordinary ultrasonic tanks aren’t designed for flammable liquids: don’t pour alcohol into them, only a fluid permitted by the cleaner’s manual. If in doubt, clean with a brush.

Drying is done slowly and gently: with warm air at about 50–60 °C for several hours, not with a hot-air station. Moisture leaves from under the chips slowly. Power up for the first time only when the board is dry, from a bench power supply with current limiting, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench.
Restoring traces
Find the break with a continuity test. Check the vias too — the plated holes that connect the board layers: corrosion eats them from the inside.
Scrape the solder mask off the ends of the trace with a scalpel down to clean copper and tin them — coat them with a thin layer of solder.

Solder in a jumper of thin insulated wire along the shortest path. In power circuits — power, grounds, injector and coil outputs — the wire’s cross-section must be no smaller than the trace’s, otherwise it will overheat.
Secure the jumper against vibration with a drop of glue or coating, and check it: it has continuity, and there’s no short to neighboring traces.
If a trace has rotted away near the connector and you can’t see where it went, don’t connect it “by eye” — check against the car’s wiring diagram and a good board.
Vibration and cracked solder joints

Heavy components — electrolytic capacitors, chokes, power transistors, on-board relays — and the connector pins rock from vibration for years, heating up and cooling down. A ring-shaped crack forms around the lead, and the contact comes and goes. This happens especially often on trucks — Shacman, Howo, KAMAZ.
Symptom: the fault appears over bumps, when cold or when hot, and goes away by itself.
Under a magnifier you can see a thin dark ring around the lead, and the solder joint looks dull.
On the bench, with the module powered on, tap the board lightly with a plastic stick while watching the current and communication; gentle heating or cooling of the area also helps.
The repair isn’t a drop of solder on top: the old solder is removed and the lead is resoldered with flux.
Conformal coating and the root cause

During repair, the factory conformal coating is removed only where you solder. After the repair, the board is cleaned of flux, dried and coated with PCB conformal coating, keeping it off the connector contacts, the programmer pads and the sensor openings. The module is installed once the coating has dried — per the coating’s instructions. But coating is no substitute for finding the cause: replace the seal, clear the drain, seal the connector and explain to the customer where the water came from. Otherwise the module will be back within a season.
A wet module is never powered up: corrosion progresses faster under voltage.
Cleaning — with alcohol and a brush; ultrasonic — with caveats and no flammable liquids; drying — slowly and gently.
A jumper in a power circuit must be no thinner than the trace; secure it and check it for shorts.
Vibration cracks are resoldered from scratch; after the repair — conformal coating and eliminating the source of moisture.
A module from a car with a flooded interior has been brought to the bench. What must you not do first?
Photograph the board
Apply power to see whether it’s alive
Inspect the board under a magnifier
Under voltage, moisture acts as an electrolyte, and corrosion progresses faster. Inspection, cleaning and drying come first.
What’s the danger of pouring isopropyl alcohol into an ordinary ultrasonic cleaner?
None, everyone does it
Alcohol is worse at removing corrosion
The cleaner isn’t designed for flammable liquids — a fire is possible
Alcohol dissolves the copper traces
Ordinary ultrasonic cleaners aren’t meant for flammable liquids. Only use what the cleaner’s manual permits.
A jumper is used to restore an output stage’s power trace. What wire should you use?
One with a cross-section no smaller than the trace’s
The thinnest one — it’s neater
Any wire, as long as it has continuity
A high current flows through a power circuit. A thin wire will overheat and burn through.

Soldering and replacing components

How to recognize SMD parts and chip packages, choose the flux and temperature, remove and install a part with a hot-air station and a soldering iron without overheating the board and neighboring parts, and why BGA is a separate story.

Almost any module repair ends with soldering: a burnt-out driver, a leaking capacitor, a crack at a lead. You can ruin a board in seconds — overheat it, tear off a pad, blow away neighboring parts. Good soldering is preparation, the right flux and patience. We covered the tools in the lesson on the workbench.
What’s on the board

SMD parts are surface-mount devices; they’re soldered onto pads with no holes. Resistors often have numbers on them: “103” means 10 followed by three zeros, that is, 10 kΩ. Capacitors usually have no markings — their values are taken from an identical good board.

Transistors and drivers come in small three-lead packages (SOT-23) or in power packages with a wide heat-sinking pad underneath (DPAK). The pad is soldered to large copper areas, so these parts are the hardest to remove.
Chips: SOIC — leads on two sides at a 1.27 mm pitch; QFP — leads on all four sides at a finer pitch, often 0.5–0.8 mm.
Replace with the same part or a full equivalent in value, package, voltage, current and temperature. Better still — automotive grade, AEC-Q qualified.
Flux, solder, temperature
Flux cleans oxides off the metal and helps the solder flow. For boards — no-clean or rosin flux gel. Soldering acid and active fluxes are no good: their residue eats away the traces.
Factory solder is often lead-free and harder to melt. A little ordinary tin-lead solder helps melt it.
A soldering iron for ordinary solder is usually set to 300–350 °C; for lead-free solder and massive leads — higher, with a thick tip. The tip stays on the lead for seconds, not tens of seconds.
Hot-air station: choose the temperature and airflow according to the station’s manual and the size of the part, starting low. Strong airflow blows away small parts.
Desoldering braid — copper braid with flux — removes excess solder. Press it down with the tip and don’t rub: it’s easy to tear off a pad.
Removing and installing
Photograph the spot and note the chip’s pin 1 mark and the polarity of the capacitor and diode.
Shield the neighboring parts — plastic connectors, electrolytic capacitors, the crystal — with Kapton tape or a foil shield.

Small parts are removed with two soldering irons, hot tweezers or a hot-air station with a narrow nozzle. SOIC and QFP — with hot air, heating all the leads evenly, or with a low-melting alloy such as Rose’s metal: it keeps the leads molten longer. Lift the part only when all the leads have melted, otherwise you’ll tear off the pads.
Clean the pads with desoldering braid and flux. Remove the low-melting alloy completely — it makes the solder joint brittle.

New part: tin one pad, place the part with tweezers and tack one lead — on a chip, two opposite corners. Check that all the leads are on their pads, solder the rest, and remove any bridges with the braid.
Wash off the flux with alcohol and check under a magnifier: each lead has a smooth, shiny fillet — a smooth transition of solder onto the pad — with no bridges or solder balls.
This is especially true for soldering: a tip free of carbon buildup, a clean hot-air nozzle, fresh flux. You can’t solder well with a dirty tip, even on an expensive station.
How not to overheat the board
A multilayer board with thick copper soaks up heat. Bottom preheating — a heater under the board — evens out the temperature, so you need less heat from above.
Signs of overheating: a darkened or blistered board, lifted pads, shifted neighboring parts. Stop and let the board cool down.
A board that has been in water is dried first, as in the lesson on moisture: with sudden heating, moisture can delaminate the board and the components.
Don’t hold the hot air on one spot longer than necessary, and don’t heat a plastic connector — it will warp.
BGA is a separate story

On a BGA, the leads are solder balls under the chip package; you can’t see them or check them with a magnifier. Replacing one requires a station with bottom preheating and a thermal profile — a set heating and cooling curve — stencils for reballing, experience, and an X-ray for inspection. A BGA processor stores the program: after replacement it has to be programmed, and without a memory backup, which is covered in the next lesson, the module can’t be restored. Don’t take on BGA until you’re confidently replacing QFP chips, and don’t believe videos that make it look easy.

Flux fumes are harmful — work with fume extraction. After working with lead-containing solder, wash your hands and don’t eat at your workbench. Keep the soldering iron only in its stand, and don’t unplug the hot-air station right away: the station has to cool the handpiece down in cool-down mode.
For boards — no-clean or rosin flux; never acid.
A part is removed when all the leads have melted; pads are cleaned with braid, not rubbed.
Neighboring parts are shielded with Kapton or foil; bottom preheating reduces the heat needed from above.
BGA is a job for proper equipment and experience; the processor is programmed after replacement.

Acid residue keeps eating away at the traces and leads. Boards need no-clean or rosin fluxes.

Exactly 10 seconds after you start heating
When the flux starts smoking
When the leads on one side have melted
If some leads are still holding, the pads will tear off with them. Lift the chip only after everything has fully melted.
An SMD resistor is marked “103”. What is its value?
10 kΩ
The first two digits are the value, the third is the number of zeros: 10 and three zeros — 10,000 Ω.

BGA soldering can’t be checked by eye, and it needs precise heating. The program is stored in the processor, so without a memory backup the module can’t be restored.
Module memory and backups
What’s stored in flash and EEPROM, why a full backup is made before any repair, how memory is read, why checksums need checking, and which memory jobs we refuse to do.

A module’s memory holds not just the program but also data specific to this car: the VIN, the immobilizer pairing, adaptations. Lose them, and you turn a repaired module into one from somebody else’s car. So there’s one rule: before soldering, flashing or changing anything on the board, make a backup.
What is stored where

Flash is program memory. It holds the module’s program and calibrations — the tables it uses to control the engine: fuel delivery, ignition timing, sensor thresholds. It’s usually built into the processor, sometimes it’s a separate chip.
EEPROM is memory for data that changes: the VIN, immobilizer data, adaptations, fault codes, equipment coding, counters. Sometimes it’s a small separate chip, sometimes part of the processor.
The bootloader is a small service program that runs first and can accept a new program. Modules are flashed through it.
Backup first
Read all the memory areas your equipment supports: flash, EEPROM and the rest. The program alone isn’t enough — it’s the EEPROM that’s unique to the car.
Read it again and compare the files. If they match, the read is reliable.
Check the file: its size equals the memory capacity, and it isn’t all FF or 00 inside. A file like that means the memory wasn’t read or is empty.
Label the files — make, VIN, module numbers, date — and store them in two places. This is customer data; it isn’t shared with outsiders.
Only after that, start the repair.
How memory is read
Via diagnostics — through the diagnostic connector or the diagnostic line, without opening the module. Convenient, but not all modules and not all areas can be read this way.

On the bench via the bootloader — the module is connected to a bench power supply and to the adapter over CAN or K-line, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. Sometimes entering the bootloader requires a service contact on the board. This usually gives a more complete read.

With a programmer on the board — to the processor’s debug interface (BDM, JTAG and the like) or directly to the memory chip: on the board contacts, with a clip, sometimes by removing the chip. The most complete method, but it requires a precise connection.
How to connect and what to press — per the manual for your programmer or tool. Power must be stable: from a bench power supply only, not from a battery charger or a run-down battery.
Checksums

A checksum is a number calculated from the memory contents and stored alongside them. At startup, the module recalculates it and compares. If it doesn’t match, the module considers the program corrupted: it won’t start, goes into limp mode or waits to be flashed. That’s why, after writing, you always verify what was written against the file — almost every programmer has a verify function. Write only your own verified file or an official update from the manufacturer. Someone else’s file from the internet may be from a different module version and contain another car’s data.
What we don’t do
We touch immobilizer data and the VIN only when there are documents for the car: the registration certificate and the owner’s ID or a power of attorney. And some jobs we always refuse.
Disabling the immobilizer, so-called “immo off”: it makes the car easier to steal.
Changing the mileage: it deceives the next buyer.
Software removal of EGR, the diesel particulate filter (DPF), AdBlue/SCR: the car emits more harmful substances, doesn’t meet environmental requirements and may fail its vehicle inspection.

Such modifications break the law and the requirements for the vehicle, and the person who made them is responsible for them. If the engine fails, there’s an accident or the car is stolen because a system was disabled, the questions will go to the technician. Refuse directly and offer to find and fix the real cause — a faulty sensor, valve or wiring.
Flash holds the program and calibrations, EEPROM holds this car’s data: the VIN, immobilizer, adaptations.
Before any repair — a backup of all areas, read twice and compared.
After writing — verify what was written; we write only our own file or an official update.
Immobilizer and VIN — only with documents; immo off, mileage changes, EGR, DPF, AdBlue removal — we don’t do these.
What is unique to a specific car and is most often stored in EEPROM?
The VIN, immobilizer data and adaptations

The bootloader

The program in memory doesn’t change between reads. Different files point to a bad contact, a voltage sag or a communication glitch.

Replacing a module with another one
When a module gets replaced, how new, remanufactured and used units differ, what has to match, what needs to be transferred and adapted, and why “just putting in a used module” often doesn’t work.

Sometimes a module can’t be repaired: the board is burnt out, the processor is damaged, corrosion has eaten too much. Then it gets replaced. But a control module isn’t a light bulb: putting in another one and starting the car right away rarely works.
First make sure the module is faulty

Many “dead” modules are actually fine: they’re short of power, ground or communication. Check this at the connector, as in the lessons on ECU power and grounds and on a module that won’t communicate. And find out what killed the old module: if the cause is a short in the wiring, the new one will burn out the same way, as in the lesson on output stages.
New, remanufactured or used
New — from the manufacturer or a dealer. The most predictable and the most expensive. It often comes without a program or with a basic one, and needs flashing and pairing at the dealer.
Remanufactured — repaired by a specialist shop, with its own warranty. It’s important that it’s prepared for your car, not sent “as is”.
Used — from a salvage yard. The cheapest of all, but its history is unknown: it may have been flooded, overheated or already repaired. And it contains another car’s data.
What has to match
The module number — the hardware number on the housing label. Modules that look identical but have different numbers are different inside.
The software number and version. With the same hardware, the program may be for a different engine, power output, transmission or emissions class.
Equipment: manual or automatic, air conditioning, cruise control and other options the module has to “know” about.

Market. For right-hand-drive Japanese cars, a module from the same model for a different market may have a different program and immobilizer. On Shacman, Howo and FAW, a module from the same Weichai or Cummins engine but with a different power rating also has a different program.
What to transfer and adapt

If the old module still communicates, before replacing it record its coding and parameters with the scan tool and save a memory backup, as in the lesson on module memory. They make it easier to set up the new one.

Immobilizer pairing: the module has to recognize this car’s keys and immobilizer unit. It’s done at the dealer or following the manufacturer’s procedure, with the right equipment and only with the car’s documents; a PIN code and all the keys are often needed.
VIN and coding — writing the car’s data and its equipment into the module following the manufacturer’s procedure.

Adaptations — teaching the module to the car: throttle position, idle, and on some cars the crankshaft sensor. On Common Rail diesels — injector codes: each injector has its own correction code, which is entered into the module with the scan tool.
Updating the program to the current version, if the manufacturer has released one.
Clear the codes in all modules and check the car — that’s covered in the next lesson.
Why “just putting in a used one” doesn’t work
The immobilizer doesn’t recognize the keys: the engine won’t start or stalls after a second or two.
A program for a different engine, transmission or market: fault codes, poor running, limp mode.
No injector codes and adaptations: rough running, smoke, fault codes.
On some makes, a used module can’t be paired using the standard procedure — only a new one will do. Check this before buying.

We don’t pair modules and keys without documents for the car, and we don’t “disable the immobilizer so a used module will work”. The immobilizer is anti-theft protection, and jobs like that help car thieves. No documents — we don’t start the job.
Before replacing, make sure the module is faulty, and fix the cause in the wiring.
The module number, program, equipment and market must match.
After installation — immobilizer pairing at the dealer or following the manufacturer’s procedure, coding, adaptations, injector codes.
A used module often won’t work without setup; pairing — only with documents.

Testing after repair and handing over to the customer
How to test a module on the bench and in the car, give it an extended run, put together a report with photos of the board, agree on the warranty, and what to record for yourself.

A module repair isn’t finished when the soldering iron cools down. It’s finished by a bench test, a test in the car and a clear report for the customer. Better to catch an intermittent fault at your shop than a week later out on the highway.
Bench test
Current draw — the same as a good module of this type, with no jumps. How to evaluate it — in the lesson on connecting on the bench.
Communication with the scan tool and identification: the module and software numbers are the same as before the repair.
Memory: compare it with the backup. The data shouldn’t have changed unless you restored it.
Outputs — with a load simulator and an oscilloscope, as in the lesson on output stages.

Extended run: the module runs under power for a long time — for intermittent faults, hours, not minutes. After a repair for moisture or cracked solder joints, tap lightly on the housing and warm it up moderately: the fault shouldn’t come back.
Testing in the car
Installation: ignition off, battery negative disconnected, connector clean, seal in place, latch closed, module secured.
Turn on the ignition and read the codes in all modules. While the module was removed, other modules often log communication codes for it: write them down, clear them and check again.
Starting: the immobilizer allows the start, and the engine starts without long cranking.
Live data: temperature, rpm, throttle position and pressures are plausible; system voltage with the engine running is 13.5–14.5 V.
Load: turn on the headlights, fans and A/C, and check the outputs you repaired. Then a test drive — under the conditions in which the fault used to show up.
After the drive, read the codes in all modules once more.

If the module used to fail in the cold, a check in a warm service bay isn’t enough. Leave the car outside overnight and check the cold start in the morning: in winter this quickly shows whether everything is in order.

Don’t look at the scan tool while driving: the driver watches the road, and a helper watches the data or the scan tool records it. And don’t disconnect the battery with the engine running “to test the alternator” — the voltage spike can damage the module you’ve just repaired.
Customer report
The complaint in the customer’s words and what you found: what fault was on the board and which measurements confirmed it.
Photos of the board before and after: corrosion, a burnt-out driver, restored traces.
What was replaced and repaired.
The cause in the car and what was done about it: a short in the wiring, water through a seal, a clogged drain. If the customer declined to fix the cause, write that down.
Recommendations and warranty terms.
Warranty

You set the warranty period yourself and write it on the work order. It covers the repair performed and the parts installed. Agree in advance on what voids it: water getting in again, a cause in the wiring that the customer chose not to fix, the module being opened by other technicians, flashing or modifying the program by third parties, welding on the body without disconnecting the modules. Put your own mark on the housing — a sticker or a marking — so you can recognize your module.
What to record for yourself
The car, the VIN, the module and software numbers.
The complaint, what you found and where: the component reference designators — the labels on the board like R12 or C5 — what you replaced them with and where you bought it.
Current draw before and after the repair, test results.
Backup files — labeled, in two places.
Handover date and warranty period. After a year, this log will become your knowledge base on modules, as in the lesson on the profession.
On the bench: current, communication and numbers, memory compared with the backup, outputs, extended run.
In the car: codes in all modules, starting, live data, load and a test drive, codes once more.
Customer report — with photos of the board before and after, the cause in the car and the warranty terms.
For yourself — the numbers, what was replaced, the measurements, memory backups and the warranty date.

A code of 2–3 digits: each digit — a series of flashes, with a pause between digits. Each code is repeated 3 times, then the next one, in ascending order of numbers.

A two-digit code: the first series of flashes — the first digit, pause, the second series — the second digit (for example, 1 flash, pause, 4 flashes = “1,4”). Only one error is shown — the most important one.

A two-digit code: the first digit — 1–8 flashes, a pause of 1,5 s, the second digit — 1–6 flashes, then a pause of 4 s and the next code. The first digit — what is faulty (2 modulator, 3 sensor gap, 4 sensor open/short circuit, 5 unstable signal/tyre size, 6 toothed rotor, 7 system functions, 8 ABS unit). The second digit for codes 2–6 — the location: 1 right front, 2 left front, 3 right rear (drive axle), 4 left rear, 5 right of the additional axle, 6 left of the additional axle.
A two-digit code: first long flashes — the first digit, then short ones — the second. For example, 3 long and 2 short flashes = code 32.

A three-digit code: the first series of flashes — the first digit, a pause of about 1 s, the second series — the second digit, pause, the third series — the third digit. For example, 2 flashes — pause — 4 flashes — pause — 2 flashes = code 2-4-2. Codes are shown one per button press, after the last one the first one comes again.
A three-digit code: the first series of flashes — hundreds, after a pause — tens, after a pause — units. For example, 1 flash — pause — 2 flashes — pause — 4 flashes = code 1-2-4.
